## Abstract

Thermal Design and Control for Stratospheric Balloon-borne Telescopes

Susan Maria Fowler Redmond

Master of Applied Science

Institute for Aerospace Studies

University of Toronto

2018

Balloon-borne experiments present unique thermal design challenges. Radiation and conduction are

the predominant heat transfer mechanisms, with convection eﬀects being diﬃcult to characterize at an

altitude of 35–40 km. This greatly constrains the thermal design options and makes predicting ﬂight

thermal behaviour diﬃcult. SuperBIT aims to study weak gravitational lensing using a 0.5 m modiﬁed

Dall-Kirkham visible-to-near-UV telescope capable of achieving 0.02 ′′ stability [24]. To achieve the

theoretical resolution of 0.25 ′′ [23], mirror deformation gradients must be less than 15 nm and the

thermal environment must be stable on hour-long time scales. The 2018 test ﬂight served to collect data

for post-ﬂight characterization and to test the newly-developed heater control process. The post-ﬂight

characterization algorithm developed allows for parameter optimization, such as physical properties

or applied heat loads, based on the temperature proﬁle. An overview of the in-ﬂight heater control

performance, and extensive simulation results for the parameter-optimization-based thermal design are

presented here.

## Chapter 1

## Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

On Earth, optical telescope capabilities and image quality are limited by atmospheric seeing. Moving

out into the far-UV or far-IR the atmosphere is mainly opaque reducing the science goals achievable

by ground-based telescopes. For these reasons, space telescopes were developed to improve data qual-

ity and probe wavelengths which are out of reach for ground-based instruments. Unfortunately, space

telescopes are very costly and have very long lead times [17]. Balloon-borne telescopes oﬀer a unique

compromise in which losses and costs are signiﬁcantly reduced. They ﬂy at altitudes ranging from 30 to

45 km in the stratosphere which provides a space-like environment but maintains gravity loading as seen

by ground-based instruments. Figure 1.1 shows the transmission gain for balloon instruments between

Near-Ultraviolet (NUV) and Near-Infrared (NIR) wavelengths when compared to ground-based instru-

ments either at sea level or the Hawaii Mauna Kea site. The current Super Pressure Balloon (SPB)

ﬂight duration record is 46 days [13] but that is expected to increase as developments continue. As

with satellites, mass and power consumption are major design optimization parameters which result in a

unique thermal design challenge due to the variability and uncertainty of the instrument loading. Histor-

ically the thermal design was determined through an iterative approach, and ﬂight results were not well

analyzed or documented. Improvements to both the characterization of the stratospheric environment,

and to the ability to predict the thermal performance of balloon-borne telescopes are desired.

SuperBIT is a 0.5 m diﬀraction-limited balloon-borne telescope which aims to study galaxy–galaxy

weak gravitational lensing. The science ﬂight is designed for a 100-day ﬂight on a Super-Pressure Balloon (SPB) out of Wanaka, NZ, in 2020. Weak lensing is an important cosmological probe capable

of constraining the matter density in the universe. As light from a source galaxy travels toward an

observer, foreground galaxies and dark matter act as lenses and distort the source galaxy image. Weak

lensing is a very powerful observational probe as it makes no assumptions on the ratio between dark

matter and baryonic matter. As implied by its name, the weak lensing signal is small, making it diﬃcult

to measure. This is compounded by the fact that any source of systematic error signiﬁcantly aﬀects

the measurement. Common instrument-induced issues are the size, shape, and stability of the point

spread function (PSF). Thermal variances in the instrument can aﬀect both the shape and stability

of the PSF. Gradients across the optical surfaces can cause aberrations and time-varying temperatures

induce correlated systematics that are diﬃcult to remove. For these reasons it is imperative that the

### 1.2 Stratospheric Thermal Environment

The stratosphere starts at an altitude of 10–18 km and transitions into the mesosphere at approximately

50 km [14]. The air pressure is low at 0.1 kPa and the temperature ranges from 222 to 278 K [14]. Note

that convection cannot be assumed to be zero until approximately 0.01 Pa. An interesting characteristic

of the stratosphere is that the ambient temperature increases with increasing altitude due to absorbed

UV radiation. Due to this temperature gradient, there is little convection between stratospheric layers.

There are, however, winds within the stratospheric layers which move the balloon throughout the ﬂight.

Temperature changes throughout day–night cycles also cause altitude variations due to pressure changes

in the balloon. This ampliﬁes the temperature drop at night as the balloon sinks to a cooler layer of

the stratosphere. To mediate this, it is possible to drop ballast making the payload lighter and thus

causing the balloon to rise, but this is only done in practice when signiﬁcant altitude changes occur.

Also, since balloon-borne telescopes operate close to the Earth and their trajectory is uncontrolled,

albedo and planetshine provide large, variable heat loads. The wavelength dependence of the incident

energy combined with the uncertainty in intensity hinders the loading prediction accuracy. Historically

the conduction and convective eﬀects of the residual atmosphere have been ignored but it is not clear

that this is a suitable assumption. For these reasons, the stratosphere is a challenging environment to

operate in, and diﬃcult to characterize.

### 1.3 Results of Previous Flights

The University of Toronto Balloon Astrophysics group currently has two balloon-borne telescope projects

underway. SuperBIT is a visible-to-near-UV telescope which studies the dark matter in galaxy clusters


<!-- Page 11 -->


Chapter 1. Introduction 3

and Spider is a microwave polarimeter which maps the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Both

telescopes have unique thermal design challenges; SuperBIT requires a high level of controllability,

while Spider requires mainly passive thermal control systems to reduce power consumption. Post-ﬂight

analysis of both instruments has revealed variations between the thermal model and the in-ﬂight data

that are not fully understood. As a result, the thermal systems in many cases are over-designed and yet under-perform. The desired solution to this problem would be to develop a ﬂexible, yet robust, design

method which can both update model parameters based on ﬂight data, and optimize model parameters

based on a desired temperature proﬁle. Such a method would yield more accurate prediction and control

of the thermal behaviour of both telescopes.

Previous SuperBIT ﬂights include a 2015 ﬂight with the Centre National d’´Etudes Spatiales (CNES)

and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) out of Timmins, ON, and ﬂights in 2016 and 2018 with NASA’s

Columbia Scientiﬁc Balloon Facility (CSBF). CSBF provides a Support Instrumentation Package (SIP)

which includes communication links as well as a number of sensors which provide a unique insight

to the stratospheric thermal environment [4]. These include multiple pyranometers, IR sensors, and

thermometers which measure the solar irradiance, planetshine, and free air temperature respectively.

Using these data as an input to the thermal model, it is possible to estimate the external heat loads on

the telescope more accurately.

### 1.4 Project and Signiﬁcance

This project is an inverse thermal control problem where the goal is to determine system thermal param-

eters given the desired outcome. These parameters can be either applied heat loads or a combination of

optical and thermophysical properties. A thermal design program capable of solving the inverse thermal

control problem would be very useful in the Balloon-borne Astronomy sector given the aforementioned

diﬃculty of characterizing balloon-borne instruments and their thermal environment.

The long term goal is to characterize thermal links, eﬀective emissivities, and component power

dissipation on the ground where the atmospheric contribution is relatively well known. These parameters

can then be used when analyzing test ﬂight data to predict the stratospheric contribution. Once this

is known, design modiﬁcations can be made to optimize the system based on the predicted conductive

and convective loading from the stratosphere. It would also allow for dynamic updating during ﬂight to

account for changes in the stratospheric load, optical properties, and heat loads. Since most telescopes

are used multiple times, ﬂight data based parameter updating facilitates quantiﬁed post ﬂight updates.

This thesis covers the development of the program to achieve this goal.

The development of this program will be primarily Matlab-based. However, it will also make use of

Thermal Desktop (TD), which has been used for past thermal analyses of both SuperBIT and Spider.

Thermal Desktop is quite powerful, and provides a convenient user interface for the development of

the physical model and mesh. TD alone does not provide the necessary customization for this project.

Therefore, a hybrid approach will be employed, in which TD will output a list of node numbers, and,

for each node, its associated subassembly, optical properties, view factors, and heat loads. This list

will then be fed into Matlab for the execution of the bulk of the analysis. The built-in calculation

of the view factors within TD, rather than in Matlab, provides a huge advantage, reducing both

complexity and computation time. This approach is justiﬁable, since the Monte Carlo ray tracer method

for the computation of view factors is a well-respected method in the ﬁeld of spacecraft thermal analysis.

Unfortunately, the thermophysical properties are not available as an output so they must be assigned to

the nodes within Matlab. This is addressed by breaking the TD model into subassemblies where each

subassembly is assigned a single material. In summary, the main objectives are the following:

• Develop a method of quantifying the acceptable temperature gradients on the SuperBIT telescope

• Improve the in-ﬂight heater control method

• Create a novel program which accepts an experimental or desired temperature proﬁle and calculates

the physical properties or heat loads

• Develop a representative model to test the program performance and capabilities

### 2.1 Weak Lensing

### 2.1.1 Weak Lensing as a Cosmological Probe

Cosmology studies the large scale evolution of the universe. Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) is the most

widely accepted model and assumes the universe contains radiation, matter, and dark energy. Each of

these components drive the temporal evolution of the universe as described by the Friedmann equation:

H2 = H2 0 � ΩRa−4 + ΩMa−3 + Ωka−2 + ΩΛ  , (2.1)

where the density parameters of each component, Ωi, relate the scale factor a of the universe – its size

– with its expansion rate H = ˙a/a and its current value H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km s−1Mpc−1 [21]. Since

there is currently no theoretical understanding of why these parameters have their speciﬁc values in our

Universe, the model parameters must be determined observationally; weak lensing provides a method of

constraining the matter density ΩM.

As previously mentioned, SuperBIT’s main science goal is to measure galaxy-galaxy weak gravita-

tional lensing for 100 clusters. This type of weak lensing uses galaxies at diﬀerent redshifts; a galaxy far,

far away as the source and a nearby galaxy cluster as the lens. The mass of the near galaxy cluster acts

as a gravitational lens and bends the light rays as shown by the white lines in Figure 2.1. Strong lensing

occurs when the lens galaxy is suﬃciently massive that it creates multiple images of the source galaxy

as shown by the red lines in Figure 2.1. Weak lensing is based on the same mechanism but produces

a milder distortion the image of the source galaxy shown in Figure 2.2 thats for illustrative purposes

only. The resulting image(s) depends on the not-necessarily-symmetric geometry of the whole system.

A perfectly symmetric system will create a single Einstein ring. Strong lensing is much more rare due

to the mass required to produce it, making weak lensing a more favourable observational probe.

Eagle Nebula taken during a SuperBIT engineering ﬂight in 2016 with the Hubble Space Telescope’s

*Figure 2.4: The Bullet Cluster [15]*

Due to this unique beneﬁt, weak lensing provides a potential method of determining the mass density

of the universe, ΩM, and the amplitude of the mass power spectrum, σ8. As discussed above these are

important cosmological parameters for the widely used ΛCDM model of the universe.

### 2.1.2 Weak Lensing Measurement Error

Weak gravitational lensing is prone and sensitive to both statistical and systematic errors. One approach

for mitigating statistical errors is to restrict the scale at which the lensing signal is measured to the scale

at which the signal becomes comparable to the noise [27]. This is due to the issues that arise at either

extreme. At large scales there are fewer modes available to measure, and thus an increase in sample


<!-- Page 16 -->


Chapter 2. Background and Theoretical Basis 8

variance uncertainty. On the other hand, at small scales shape noise from the telescope beam begins

to dominate, decreasing the ability to measure the lensing signal. Another common issue is accurately

determining the redshift of the source galaxy. This is nominally done using photometric redshifts which

use crude ﬁlters and depend on strong features such as the Balmer break. This can be problematic as

the Lyman-α (Ly-α) feature can also be redshifted to the point that it appears to be the Balmer break, which is known as “photo-z degeneracy” [27]. A 1% change in the redshift of the source galaxy leads to

a 2% change in the power spectrum hence the source redshift must be known to the sub-percent level

[27]. The uncertainty in the source galaxy redshift can be reduced by using narrower ﬁlter bands over

a wider range such that both the Balmer and Ly-α features are visible or by comparing measurements

with large redshift surveys.

Instrument imperfections also contribute to errors in the weak lensing measurement. Misaligning or

over-constraining the optical surfaces can drastically aﬀect the point spread function (PSF). The PSF

describes the 2D intensity pattern that results when a point source is mapped to the image plane by the

telescope optics. If the PSF is not isotropic it can appear as a weak lensing signal as shown in Figure 2.5.

Imperfections in the optical surfaces as well as the wavelength-dependent nature of coatings cause the

PSF to change across the focal plane. Due to the ﬁnite number of stars in the sky, the PSF cannot be

characterized on every point on the focal plane thus interpolation is required. This interpolation can be

unconstrained so instrument models and heuristic methods are often used in parallel [27]. By dithering

the telescope between exposures, SuperBIT moves the image slightly on the focal plane, which further

facilitates characterization of the systematics.

*Figure 2.5: Eﬀect of PSF [10]*

In addition to changing across the focal plane, the PSF also changes with wavelength [27]. Repeating

observations in multiple bands using relatively narrow ﬁlters can aid in removing this systematic in the

post-processing. The last important PSF parameter is its overall size. As the PSF size increases with

respect to the galaxy size on the focal plane it dilutes the ellipticity measurement and increases the

required observing time [27].

When the images are corrected for the estimated systematics it is also possible to perform null tests

to check the correction success. One such test is to compute the correlation function between the PSF-

corrected galaxies and the star ellipticities in the original image [27]. Correlation between the two is a

good indicator that residual instrument systematics exist in the image.

### 2.2 The Parameter Updating Problem

When designing the thermal aspect of systems, the most common or traditional technique uses compo-

nent temperatures as the unknown parameters. Material properties as well as external heat loads are

used to calculate the temperature proﬁle of the system. If the proﬁle deviates from what is desired,

passive or active thermal control devices are implemented until the results are acceptable. Though this

has proven to be eﬀective it can be time consuming and requires an in depth understanding of heat

transfer and thermodynamics to be able to interpret the results and make eﬀective updates between

iterations. For these reasons, the inverse thermal design approach was introduced.

NASA uses two approaches within their Integrated Modeling of Optical Systems (IMOS) tool de-

veloped at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) [19]. Both concepts require the desired temperature

proﬁle as an input. One option is to input the thermophysical properties and solve for the required

additional heat loads, also known as the thermal control problem [19]. This is useful when the phys-

ical properties are well known, which is not always the case in the stratosphere or with sub-optimal

component contacts. The next option is to specify the heat loads and solve for the properties, or the

parameter updating problem [19]. This method is most applicable in radiation dominated environments

where optical properties can be customized with relative ease which is directly applicable to SuperBIT

and Spider. In both cases Papalexandris and Milman [19] prove that for a given temperature gradient

there is a unique set of parameters which are required. Ideally these two concepts will be combined for

this project to facilitate thermal control optimization.

There have also been methods developed to extrapolate experimental temperature proﬁle data to the

full thermal model [20]. Based on this approach, data from test ﬂights and thermal vacuum tests can

be used along with the previously discussed methods to update parameters creating a more accurate

model. Though they are still relatively new, they have been tested and found to be robust. In addition

to extrapolation techniques, understanding the thermal sensitivity of important components can aid

thermal design. Providing the model is accurate, it indicates the critical parameters that must be pre-

cisely implemented to maintain components within their respective allowable ranges. Many approaches

have been developed; the main one involves calculating the partial derivatives of the nodal equations

with respect to the design parameters [5]. Though the equations are nonlinear in temperature, they are

linear with respect to most design parameters including conductivity and external heat loads reducing

the complexity of the problem. It is also useful for parameter updating and thermal control problems

as providing the gradient of the objective function to the nonlinear solver can decrease the run time

and increase accuracy. It must be acknowledged that for SuperBIT the environment ﬂuctuates with the

day-night cycles and the irregular slew patterns when pointing at galaxy clusters. For this reason, the

sensitivities may change with time with some parameters being critical during the day and others during

the night.

### 2.3 Optimization Methods

Many of the aforementioned methods can be solved using a built in Matlab Sequential Quadratic

Programming (SQP) function fmincon [11]. SQP is a very powerful iterative technique which optimizes

a quadratic model of the objective function subject to a linearization of the constraints [25]. At each

iteration the Hessian is calculated which is deﬁned as the second gradient of the Lagrangian. The Hessian

Beneﬁts of this approach include the strict adherence to bounds, robustness with respect to non-double

results, and reformulated feasibility routines when constraints are not met [25]. The input to fmincon can be expressed as:

### 2.4 The Thermal Balance Equation

### 2.4.1 Governing Equation Derivation

The governing equation for a thermal system in steady state is simply a statement of the ﬁrst law of

thermodynamics; heat in must equal heat out. This is generally expressed as:

X Qext = Qradiation + Qconduction + Qconvection (2.5)

For a given node, the sum of the applied heat loads must equal the heat leaving the node via radiation,

conduction, and convection. In the stratosphere due to the low air density and large convective cell size,

convection is typically neglected. This will be revisited in the future as it is believed that this is a poor

assumption but including it was not needed for proof of concept for this project. Also, since it is the

combined conduction and convective coeﬃcient that is desired, it is a linear contribution and will be

very easy to add back in for future developments. This equation can be arranged in an alternate format

more convenient for iterative solvers:

F(ϵ, k, α, qh) = Qradiation + Qconduction − X Qext = 0 (2.6)

External heat loads can either come from a heater, incident solar ﬂux, albedo, or planetshine. Heater

### 2.5 Thermal Desktop

### 2.5.1 Program Overview

Thermal Desktop (TD) is a ﬁnite diﬀerence based AutoCAD add on produced by C&R Technologies R ⃝

designed to meet the needs of spacecraft thermal design. It can handle conduction, convection, and

radiative heat transfer as well as containing many external heat load options. TD allows the user to

specify an orbit and can then generate the albedo, planetshine, and solar heat loads. If desired, the user

can also input the albedo at each time step for the orbit which is useful for post ﬂight analysis. TD

also provides the option to plot power into a node from diﬀerent sources. This is very important when

verifying that sun-shields or sun sensors function as planned for desired scan strategies. Some useful TD

features that are sometimes overlooked are listed below.

• Display heating rates from particular sources

– Useful for verifying that sunshield is functioning

– Can help predict ground pick-up

• Drive symbols from excel

– Deﬁne all heat loads and heater states as symbols

– User can then have heat loads etc in an external spreadsheet which is easier for tracking and

updating

– Also allows user to load diﬀerent symbol values for diﬀerent case sets rather than manually

changing values

• Colour by Property

– Allows user to eﬃciently check if correct physical properties have been assigned

– Especially useful if surface has diﬀerent properties on either side

• Analyze Heaters From Results

– Outputs the PWM percentage of the heater based on the available power deﬁned

– Allows user to verify heater power has suﬃcient margin

• Import

– STEP geometry can be exported from other CAD software and imported into TD

– The user can then use the STEP geometry to re-create the model using TD objects

### 2.5.2 Thermal Desktop Radiation Calculations

The radiation calculations are executed in TD by the RadCAD R ⃝function. TD calculates the radia-

tive energy exchanged between two nodes, deﬁned as “radks”[18], using the Monte Carlo method as a

“stochastic integration technique”[18]. Rays are isotropically and randomly shot from a given node and

traced around the model as they strike other surfaces. To maintain consistency between simulation runs,

the software allows the user to request that the same random sample is used at the start of each run.

The change in ray energy as it propagates is dependent on the optical properties deﬁned for the model

surfaces. It is important to note that if a surface face is set as ‘inactive’ the ray energy is altered as per

the emissivity of the inactive face but the change in energy is not applied to the node. If the emissivity

is set to unity the ray energy goes to zero when it strikes the inactive face; if it is set to zero the ray is

perfectly reﬂected. Setting the emissivity to zero is not recommended as it can lead to inﬁnite loops.

For active faces in the basic case, each ray’s energy is decremented by the absorptivity of each surface

it encounters until it reaches a user speciﬁed minimum (the ‘Energy CutoﬀFraction’) and is terminated.

The user speciﬁed minimum prevents the program from getting stuck in an inﬁnite loop but can also

produce inaccurate results if it is set too high. TD oﬀers an alternative which treats an absorptivity as

a probability that a ray will be completely absorbed. To implement this option the user must set the

‘Energy CutoﬀFraction’ value to one. When a ray encounters a surface it is either fully absorbed or

fully reﬂected with it’s energy unchanged. The ray tracing continues until all rays are absorbed. This

can be more CPU eﬃcient but tends to distribute the error non-uniformly with the error increasing with

distance from the emitting node. Note that this is only applied during radk calculation and not view

factor calculation. For both approaches it is obvious that the accuracy of the result is heavily dependant

on the number of rays shot by each node. If the average radk magnitude is known, the error for an

individual radk can be predicted using:

Errorij = 1.65

s

1 −Bij NraysBij × 100% (2.66)

which is inversely proportional to the square root of the number of rays shot [18]. The accuracy can

be checked by looking at the ‘C#A#.xls’ ﬁle in the ‘Run #’ folder automatically created during a

simulation. The sum of all radks leaving a node should equal one i.e. a node should only emit the

amount of energy it has. Due to the numerical nature of the Monte Carlo method this is never the case.

The ‘C#A#.xls’ ﬁle lists the error in this sum which is a good benchmark for if enough rays have been

shot. The error can be reduced by a factor of two if the number of rays is quadrupled [18].

It is important to note that while TD oﬀers the functionality to calculate classic View Factors, they

are not used within the simulation unless speciﬁcally requested. When the traditional View Factor

approach is used it is assumed that a surface is uniformly loaded. By using the Monte Carlo approach

it allows the user to implement much coarser meshes as this method does not require uniform loading.

While the Monte Carlo method is powerful and eﬃcient, tracing all rays through an entire model

at once can be slow. To combat this, TD puts the model in a bounding box and divides it into eight

sub-boxes called ‘oct-cells’ as shown in Figure 2.8. It then continues to divide the oct-cells into more,

smaller oct-cells until the used speciﬁed maximum surfaces per cell is met. The result is that regions

with a denser mesh will also have more oct-cells. Once the model is suﬃciently subdivided the ray

tracing begins. The program only initially checks for collisions with surfaces within the same oct-cell as

continues until the ray energy drops below the user speciﬁed value or until the ray goes to ‘space’.

### 3.1 SuperBIT

*Figure 3.1: SuperBIT [23]*

The SuperBIT instrument is shown in Figure 3.1 and consists of three nested frames which allow

for three-axis control. The outer frame is controlled in yaw by a reaction wheel in partnership with a

pivot motor, which is used to dump excess momentum up the ﬂight train connecting the payload to the

balloon. The middle frame mates to the outer frame at the bow and the stern through two frameless

motors allowing for ±6 deg roll control. The telescope is housed in the inner frame which is controlled

in pitch with a range of 20 deg to 60 deg. This gimballed frame structure, combined with a bore-sight

star camera and encoders, make up the coarse pointing system. The coarse pointing system is used to

stabilize the telescope to within 1” and the piezo-actuated tertiary mirror further improves it by two

24

orders of magnitude to within 0.02” [23]. A roll star camera in partnership with the bore-sight star

camera is used to perform a Lost-in-Space algorithm to determine where SuperBIT aimed on the sky,

but only the bore star camera is used in the pointing solution. Fully assembled it stands three metres

tall and weighs approximately one metric tonne. A detailed description of the structural [6] and control

systems [23] designs can be found in previous publications.

As previously discussed, SuperBIT’s main science goal is to measure galaxy-galaxy weak gravitational

lensing for up to 100 clusters. Shape exposures are on the order of an hour, followed by shorter exposures

in the ﬁve photometry bands. For this observing strategy it is critical that the thermal behaviour of the

optics be extremely stable on hour timescales [22]. For the three test ﬂights (2015, 2016, and 2018), a

cost-eﬀective, semi-custom telescope was used that was suﬃcient to determine actual in-ﬂight stability

limits, and to provide proof-of-concept imaging. For the science ﬂight a fully custom, high quality

instrument has been designed which accounts for the unique SuperBIT requirements. This telescope will

be integrated and tested on the ground in late 2018.

### 3.3 Thermal Control

The results discussed in this section are also published in reference [22].

### 3.3.1 Thermal control of SuperBIT Optics in the Stratosphere

Thermal control of optical surfaces is a well known challenge in astronomy. Static deformations on the

order of 15 nm and varying deformations over time can result in misleading weak gravitational lensing

measurements. It is thus desired to house the instrument in a static, isothermal environment and to have a well designed telescope which allows the optics to contract freely at ﬂoat. SuperBIT has a 1.9m

long temperature controlled baﬄe to maintain the optics at 273 K, rather than the ambient 233 K,

for the test ﬂights due to the thermal masses of the mirrors, sub-par mirror mounts, and steady state

temperature of the tertiary mirrors. The large thermal masses of the primary and secondary mirrors

require a setpoint temperature which allows them to stabilize post-launch in a reasonable amount of

time. It was predicted that the sub-optimal design of the engineering telescope would excessively deform

the mirrors if they were permitted to cool to the ambient 233 K. The science telescope will be installed

after the 2018 test ﬂight making this concern largely obsolete. Lastly, the optics box housing the tertiary

or tip-tilt mirror, shown in Figure 3.2, nominally reaches a temperature 273 K when the baﬄe heaters

are oﬀ. It is beneﬁcial to have all optics at the same temperature so 273 K was a logical setpoint.

The secondary mirror is enclosed in an aluminum housing reducing the eﬀectiveness of the temperature


<!-- Page 37 -->


Chapter 3. SuperBIT Instrument Study 29

controlled baﬄe. A heater is attached to a radiator plate located behind the secondary mirror which

provides additional control while avoiding gradients across the optical surface.

During the The 100 day SPB ﬂight from Wanaka, NZ, SuperBIT will experience extreme day and

night temperature conditions causing many of SuperBIT’s electrical and mechanical components to

require heaters. As of the 2018 test ﬂight there are a total of 30 heaters on the payload and each

heater is controlled using a standard proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control loop. To minimize

power and increase thermal stability, it is desired to have individual PID gains for each heater. As

previously discussed, the stratospheric environment is not well characterized so PID gains tuned on the

ground are not necessarily well suited to ﬂoat conditions. Also, for components with a large thermal

mass, tuning gains can take upwards of an hour. Manually tuning 30 heaters is thus time consuming

and impractical for a test ﬂight scenario where time is limited. For this reason an auto-tuning feature

has been implemented. Each heater-themistor-component system is modelled as an equivalent thermal

resistor-capacitor (RC) circuit, and a least-squares optimizer is used to ﬁnd the PID gains which minimize

overshoot and settling time. This is done using Matlab’s sequential quadratic programming function

fmincon described in Section 2.3. This function is relatively robust with respect to local minima and

invalid guesses.

### 3.3.3 Heater Control Loop

The heaters are controlled using a simple PID control loop. First, the error (E), integrated error (IE),

and change in error (dE) are computed between the setpoint and current temperature. Each error measurement is weighted by a gain, where Kp is the proportional gain, Ki is the integral gain, and Kd is the derivative gain. The result is then used to determine the percent of total power applied by the

heater. The optimization loop uses a time step h which can be diﬀerent from the 100 Hz ﬂight PID loop

to be incorporated into any term dependant on the time step. To ensure long term stability, the current

value of the error is de-weighted when calculating the integral. This ensures that sporadic temperature

or readout spikes do not drive the power request as this can result in a negatively damped system. The

current temperature error receives a weight of a and the integrated error from the previous time step

receives a weight of b which are empirically calibrated values:

### 3.3.4 Heater Gain Auto-tune Methodology

The general process for auto-tuning the heater PID gains is as follows:

Step 1: The component heater is turned on at 100% power until the thermistor sees a temperature

increase of a certain amount, at which point it is turned oﬀ. Temperature and heater power data (Tdat and Qdat) are recorded until the component returns to its original temperature. The magnitude of the

increase is chosen to be ∼2 K for components with a large thermal mass (∼104 J/K) and ∼4 K for

components with a small thermal mass (∼100 J/K). These ∆T values were empirically determined to

produce an adequate curve for the optimizer to ﬁt as it works best using a ﬁne time step (∼0.2 s) and

a shorter total time.

Output: Tdat, Qdat

Step 2: The thermal circuit parameters and optimal PID gains are determined.

Step 2a: The solver is run using the recorded heater proﬁle to determine thermal resistances and

capacitances of the system.

### 4.1 Thermal Desktop–Matlab Interface

### 4.1.1 Interface Overview

To implement this approach, the model is ﬁrst drawn in Thermal Desktop. The model can be validated

by running a simulation which includes ground atmospheric conditions and comparing the results to

data from ground operations. From here, various aspects of the thermal network can be exported taking

advantage of both TD’s aesthetic visual representation of the model and its eﬃciently implemented

Monte Carlo ray tracing technique for determining view factors between nodes. These ﬁles are then

imported into a Matlab code, where the main analysis is performed. A subset of the subassemblies

are chosen to have unknown parameters and the optimizer solves for the system that best represents

the user-deﬁned temperature proﬁle. The new temperature proﬁle and its error can then be plotted as

a colour-map in TD.

Thermal Desktop has many features that maximize the eﬃciency of the thermal design software. The

Matlab code was developed to read in the applicable TD output ﬁles in their respective formats. This

was a nontrivial task as many of the output ﬁles have variable header formats and a node numbering

technique had to be developed. In Thermal Desktop, the node numbering is local to each subassembly such that TELESCOPE.1 is diﬀerent than BALLOON.1. As such, the subassembly name must be

extracted and converted into a unique identiﬁer and then paired with the local node number. The

subassemblies are then sorted in ascending order and then paired with a simpler identiﬁer. This ensures

that the conversion is consistent for all portions of the code. All global node numbers have the same

number of digits where the ﬁrst three indicate the subassembly and the last four indicate the node

number within the subassembly; for example node 1000024 is the 24th node in subassembly 100. This

ensures the nodes stay with their subassembly when sorted. Also, surface nodes can have diﬀerent

optical properties on each side. To deal with this TD has an option to assign unique node numbers

to the top and bottom faces of surfaces. This will be a useful feature for future developments. In this

iteration of the code it was decided to keep it simple and surfaces either have the same optical properties

on both sides or they only have one side active. Since the outputs available from TD are somewhat

limiting, it was desired to set a requirement that all subassemblies must share the same conductivities

and emissivities.

Due to the awkward TD output ﬁle format, the model must be carefully assembled in a way that does

not change the ﬁle format. For this reason TD ‘contactors’ cannot be used as it changes the ‘SINDA.CC’

format. Developments in the ﬁle reader section could be done to deal with this but TD ‘conductors’

have a very similar functionality and were suﬃcient for this iteration. Furthermore, comments cannot be

added to conductors or heat loads as that to changes the ﬁle format. When a TD surface is created there

is the option to use ‘edge’ or ‘face’ contacts. This tells the program to look for surfaces touching the

applicable edge/face and apply the speciﬁed thermal resistance between the two. TD does not always

ﬁnd the contacts desired and will indicate so in the auto-generated ‘Contact Warnings.txt’ ﬁle. It is thus

recommended against using the edge or surface contact feature except in very speciﬁc circumstances.

If the two surfaces intersect it is best to create the mesh such that nodes along the intersection can

be ‘merged’ as it is much more reliable and accurate. In this iteration of the Matlab code nodes can

only be merged in TD if they are in the same subassembly as otherwise the merged node has two sets of

properties. For nodes in diﬀerent subassemblies conductors are a suitable alternative. All thermophysical properties were also assumed to be constant with respect to temperature and all surfaces are assumed

to be grey (τ = 0). Altering either of these options both creates unusable output ﬁles and a system that

of magnitude faster than fmincon for this case which is why it is used. The output of T SOLVER is

This indicates that any discrepancy is due to fundamental model diﬀerences and not a lack of optimizer

convergence.

The third section of the code is the actual optimization. Here there are two nested SQP solvers with

fmincon running the outer loop (PARAMETER SOLVER / HEATER SOLVER) and lsqnonlin used

for the inner loop (T SOLVER). Upon entering the outer loop, the vector of unknowns (x) is updated

and the corresponding temperature distribution is determined (T(x)) using T SOLVER which uses an initial guess of 200 K for all nodes. The objective function is calculated (Eq. (2.3)) followed by the

gradients as described in Section 2.4.2. The tolerances are checked with the speciﬁed values outlined in

*Table 2.2 the function exits if one of the conditions described in Table 2.3 are met; otherwise it updates*

x and runs the process again.

There are a number of situations in which the optimizer does not produce optimal results. As pre-

viously mentioned, if the exit ﬂag is less than zero an error message is prompted. The most common

error is when the optimizer cannot maintain the equality constraint in which case the failure is obvious.

Alternatively, an exit ﬂag of 2 can also be an indicator that the solution has not actually converged.

There are cases when the step size shrinks too quickly resulting in very small changes in the objective

function between steps. The solver then thinks it is at a minimum and exits. For this reason it is

sometimes better to provide an initial guess far from the predicted value to keep the steps larger for

longer. When this does occur it is fairly obvious with the output values being very similar to the initial

guess and the temperature error being on the order of 2–10 K.

In summary the algorithm:

• Imports all external ﬁles, creates global node numbering scheme, and retrieves initial desired

temperature distribution

• Creates Matlab model

– Assembles conduction area-length matrix CAL

– Assembles view factor matrix Ff

– Retrieves nodal heat load vector Qap

– Retrieves nodal k, ϵ, and α values that were used in the TD model

• Performs optimizer preprocessing

– Imports user-deﬁned unknown parameters and desired optimizer algorithm

– Assembles fmincon inputs including the initial guess vector, equality and inequality constraint

deﬁnitions, and parameter bounds

– Performs error check between TD model and Matlab model; halts progress if any nodal

temperature error is larger than 3 K

– Updates desired temperature proﬁle to Matlab prediction

• Performs parameter optimization

– Calculates temperature distribution for current parameter values

– Calculates objective function and objective function gradients

– Exits solver if tolerances are met, otherwise updates the parameter values and continues

• Calculates temperature distribution and temperature error for optimized parameters

• Calculates parameter error based on values used in TD simulation

power to the telescope. The optics box is mounted to the back plate of the telescope and contains the

science instrument and supporting electronics. It is represented here as a heat loads on the back plate

of the telescope.

To demonstrate the eﬀectiveness of the process, a number of plots are provided for representative

simulations. First is a temperature colourmap of the system using the optimized parameters output

by the Matlab algorithm. This shows that the overall distribution of heat matches the initial TD

simulation. Next there is a temperature error plot. This error plot is the absolute value of the diﬀerence

between the temperature proﬁle fed into the optimizer and that which uses the optimized parameters.

Combining this with the TD–Matlab temperature error yields the post-processed TD–Matlab error.

The last two plots are of the optimized parameter temperature proﬁle and the TD output temperature

proﬁle but the colour-bars have been rescaled to match.

In addition to the plots, a table summarizing other simulations completed is provided. The top two

rows apply to the entire table outlining the parameters and their values in the TD simulation. Since

Subassembly 3 only consists of one node, it was never included in the optimization tests. Also, since

Subassemblies 2 and 3 consist only of boundary nodes, conduction is not considered anywhere in the TD

or Matlab models so it too was ignored for the optimization tests. All conductivities are in W/m/K and

all powers are in W. The values quoted for both the Percent Error and the Maximum Terror are absolute

values. The Optimization Time is only the time for it takes optimization portion of the code takes to

run (third section in Figure 4.1); the front end of the code is not included here as it only needs to be run

once per model. The weighting scheme is generally uniform for the parameter optimization scheme but

is sometimes varied if one subassembly is performing much worse than the others. If this is the case a

weighting is applied to all nodes in that subassembly. In the heat load solver, errors associated with the

nodes with heat loads are weighted by a factor of ﬁve by default to aid in more eﬃcient convergence.

In testing this algorithm it was desired to cover a large portion of the parameter space. This was

## Conclusions and Future Work

### 5.1 Conclusions

Balloon-borne telescopes operate in very harsh and variable thermal environments. Being able to predict,

characterize, and design for the stratosphere is extremely important. Major strides have been made to

do just that for the SuperBIT instrument. Measuring galaxy–galaxy weak lensing is very diﬃcult and

imposes very strict tolerances on the optical surfaces. A preliminary analysis has been performed on the

SuperBIT primary mirror showing eﬀorts to isolate it from external loading were not suﬃcient during

the 2018 test ﬂight. This is to be updated prior to the 2019 test ﬂight and is expected to drastically

improve with the new science telescope which has been designed with this in mind.

Thermal control is an important aspect of a successful SuperBIT ﬂight. The 2018 test ﬂight imple-

mented a new approach in which the PID gains were optimized on the ground prior to the ﬂight. This

was accomplished by modelling the thermistor-heater-component system as an RC circuit for which the

parameters could be determined using the temperature response to a step input of the heater. Using

this model, the PID gains could be optimized based on the desired steady state error, settling time, and

percent overshoot. Flight data shows that the gains did not perform as well at ﬂoat as they did on the

ground but there was still a signiﬁcant improvement over previous ﬂights. In many cases the steady

state error was reduced by an order of magnitude and the oscillation amplitude was reduced by a factor

of two. This was a very successful ﬁrst implementation of the process providing a very solid foundation to build on for the next ﬂight.

To aid in thermal design a parameter estimation code has been developed. This code uses outputs

from TD to create a Matlab thermal model which is then used to optimize various aspects of the model. The Matlab model compiled from the TD outputs is not perfect and there exists a temperature error

on the order of 1 K between the two. This is the result of discrepancies between the conductances and

view factors used in the TD simulation versus what is produced in the output ﬁles. If the Matlab–TD

error is large it is an indication that there are issues with either the TD simulation settings or the TD

model. An insuﬃcient ray request in the monte carlo algorithm can very quickly cause the two models

to diverge. Also, if edge contacts are deﬁned TD does not always fully incorporate them in the output

ﬁles. Once the Matlab model is created, either the thermophysical properties can be optimized or

the heat loads. As shown in Section 4.5, the optimization algorithm is quite robust to the number of

unknowns, combinations of unknowns, as well as the initial guess. SOI studies are provided for each

# Extremal random matrices with independent entries and matrix superconcentration inequalities

**Authors:** Tatiana Brailovskaya Address: Department of Mathematics, Duke University, 120 Science Dr, Durham, NC 27710, USA Email address: tatiana.brailovskaya@duke.edu and Ramon van Handel Address: Fine Hall 207, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Email address: rvan@math.princeton.edu

## Abstract

We prove nonasymptotic matrix concentration inequalities for the spectral norm of (sub)gaussian random matrices with centered independent entries that capture fluctuations at the Tracy-Widom scale. This considerably improves previous bounds in this setting due to Bandeira and Van Handel, and establishes the best possible tail behavior for random matrices with an arbitrary variance pattern. These bounds arise from an extremum problem for nonhomogeneous random matrices: among all variance patterns with a given sparsity parameter, the moments of the random matrix are maximized by block-diagonal matrices with i.i.d. entries in each block. As part of the proof, we obtain sharp bounds on large moments of Gaussian Wishart matrices.

#### Key words and phrases:

#### 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification

## 1. Introduction

Let $X$ be an $n\times m$ matrix whose entries are independent, centered Gaussian variables with an arbitrary variance pattern $X_{ij}\sim N(0,b_{ij}^{2})$ . This paper is concerned with bounding the spectral norm $\|X\|$ of such matrices.

In the special case that $b_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$ , we recover one of the most classical models of random matrix theory: then $\|X\|^{2}=\|X^{*}X\|$ is the norm of a Wishart matrix with unit covariance. In this case, classical methods of random matrix theory yield the exact asymptotic behavior [12]

$$ \lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}n,m\to\infty\\
m=cn\end{subarray}}\mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m}+\tfrac{1}{2}(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}})^{1/3}s\big]=1-F_{1}(s), $$

where $F_{1}(s)$ is the distribution function of the Tracy-Widom law of order one. From this expression, we immediately read off that in the above asymptotic regime $\|X\|=(1+o(1))(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m})$ with fluctuations of order $n^{-1/6}\vee m^{-1/6}$ . It is important to note that the scale of the fluctuations is much smaller than what is predicted by general concentration of measure principles [14], which yield fluctuations of order $O(1)$ in the present setting. The presence of such unexpectedly small fluctuations is sometimes called the superconcentration phenomenon [7].

The Wishart model is amenable to explicit computations due to its simple structure and large degree of symmetry. However, there is little hope to perform explicit computations for an arbitrary variance pattern $(b_{ij})$ , as such models can exhibit a wide variety of different structures and behaviors that are specific to the given pattern (for example, this class includes random band matrices and sparse matrices with an arbitrary deterministic sparsity pattern as special cases). Nonetheless, given their importance in many applications, it is of considerable interest to obtain bounds for random matrices with an arbitrary variance pattern.

One of the main results in this direction was obtained some years ago by Bandeira and the second author. To describe this result, define the parameters

$$ \sigma_{1}^{2}:=\max_{j\leq m}\sum_{i\leq n}b_{ij}^{2},\qquad\quad\sigma_{2}^{2}:=\max_{i\leq n}\sum_{j\leq m}b_{ij}^{2},\qquad\quad\sigma_{*}^{2}:=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\leq n\\
j\leq m\end{subarray}}b_{ij}^{2}. $$

The following is shown in [4, Corollary 3.11].

#### Theorem 1.1 ([4]).

Let $n\leq m$ , and let $X$ be the $n\times m$ random matrix whose entries $X_{ij}\sim N(0,b_{ij}^{2})$ are independent. Then we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>(1+\varepsilon)(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2})+\sigma_{*}t\big]\leq n\,e^{-C_{\varepsilon}t^{2}} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ and $0<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , where the constant $C_{\varepsilon}$ depends only on $\varepsilon$ .

Theorem 1.1 implies that

$$ \|X\|\leq(1+\varepsilon)(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2})+C_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}\,\sigma_{*}\sqrt{\log n}\quad\text{w.h.p.} $$

In the Wishart case $b_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$ , this yields $\|X\|\leq(1+o(1))(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m})$ which captures the exact leading order behavior in (1.1). However, the order of the fluctuations in Theorem 1.1 is much larger than in (1.1): the second term in (1.3) diverges as $n,m\to\infty$ , while the second order term in (1.1) is $o(1)$ . In particular, Theorem 1.1 fails to recover any form of superconcentration.

On the other hand, the large second term in (1.3) is unavoidable in general for sparse matrices, as the following classical example illustrates.

#### Example 1.2.

Let $n=m$ and $b_{ij}=1_{|i-j|\leq k}$ , that is, $X$ is a random band matrix with bandwidth $2k+1$ . Then we have

$$ \sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}=2\sqrt{2k+1},\qquad\quad\|X\|\geq\max_{i}|X_{ii}|=(1+o(1))\sqrt{2\log n} $$

with high probability as $n\to\infty$ . It follows that the second term in (1.3) dominates the behavior of $\|X\|$ in the sparse regime $k\ll\log n$ . In fact, (1.3) optimally captures the phase transition for the leading order behavior of the norm of random band matrices (cf. [4, Corollary 4.4] in the self-adjoint case).

Such examples suggest that the large scale of the fluctuations in Theorem 1.1 is a necessary feature of any bound for random matrices with an arbitrary variance pattern. Surprisingly, this expectation turns out to be incorrect. The main results of this paper will yield a considerable improvement on Theorem 1.1, which simultaneously captures the fluctuations at Tracy-Widom scale of (1.1) and sharpens the phase transition between sparse and dense matrices that is implicit in (1.3).

### 1.1. Main results

While the main results of this paper will be proved both for non-self-adjoint and for self-adjoint random matrices, we focus the presentation in the introduction on the non-self-adjoint case for concreteness. We further consider a slightly more general setting than the above Gaussian model.

#### Model 1.3.

$X$ is an $n\times m$ matrix with $X_{ij}=b_{ij}\xi_{ij}$ , where $b_{ij}\geq 0$ are arbitrary scalars and $\xi_{ij}$ are independent symmetrically distributed real random variables with $\mathbf{E}[\xi_{ij}^{2p}]\leq\mathbf{E}[g^{2p}]$ for all $i,j$ and $p\in\mathbb{N}$ (here $g\sim N(0,1)$ ).

In the setting of Model 1.3, we always define $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{*}$ as in (1.2).

#### 1.1.1. Small deviations

Our main result in this setting is the following.

#### Theorem 1.4 (Small deviations).

Let $X$ be as in Model 1.3 and $\sigma_{1}\leq\sigma_{2}$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}+\sigma_{*}^{4/3}\sigma_{1}^{-1/3}t\big]\leq\frac{n\sigma_{*}^{2}}{C\sigma_{1}^{2}}\,e^{-Ct^{3/2}} $$

for all $0\leq t\leq\frac{\sigma_{1}^{1/3}\sigma_{2}}{\sigma_{*}^{4/3}}$ , where $C$ is a universal constant.

#### Remark 1.5.

The assumption $\sigma_{1}\leq\sigma_{2}$ entails no loss of generality, as in the opposite case $\sigma_{1}>\sigma_{2}$ we may simply apply Theorem 1.4 to the adjoint matrix $X^{*}$ .

In the Wishart case $b_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$ with $n\leq m$ , Theorem 1.4 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m}+n^{-1/6}t\big]\leq C^{-1}e^{-Ct^{3/2}} $$

for $0\leq t\leq n^{1/6}\sqrt{m}$ . This captures precisely the fluctuations and the upper tail of the Tracy-Widom asymptotics (1.1), up to a universal constant. To the best of our knowledge, the nonasymptotic bound is new even in this very special case (a slightly weaker bound in this setting may be found in [18, Theorem 2]).

For arbitrary variance patterns with $\sigma_{1}\leq\sigma_{2}$ , Theorem 1.4 yields

$$ \|X\|\leq\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}+C^{\prime}\,\frac{\sigma_{*}^{4/3}}{\sigma_{1}^{1/3}}\log^{2/3}\bigg(\frac{n\sigma_{*}^{2}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}\bigg)\quad\text{w.h.p.} $$

provided $\sigma_{1}^{1/4}\sigma_{2}^{3/4}\gtrsim\sigma_{*}\sqrt{\log n}$ . In particular, as soon as $\sigma_{1}\gg\sigma_{*}\sqrt{\log n}$ , (1.4) improves drastically on (1.3). We will explain in section 1.1.3 that this bound is essentially the best possible even for nonhomogeneous random matrices.

#### 1.1.2. Large deviations

Theorem 1.4 controls small deviations, that is, deviations up to the order of the mean. In contrast, the large deviations of $\|X\|$ are controlled by its Gaussian tail behavior [19, Corollary 3.2], and we cannot expect a qualitative improvement over Theorem 1.1 in this setting.

Nonetheless, the basic principle behind Theorem 1.4 gives rise to a quantitative improvement: a variant of Theorem 1.1 with optimal constants.

#### Theorem 1.6 (Large deviations).

Let $X$ be as in Model 1.3 and $n\leq m$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}+\sigma_{*}(1+t)\big]\leq 2n\,e^{-t^{2}/2} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ .

Theorem 1.6 implies that

$$ \|X\|\leq\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}+(1+o(1))\,\sigma_{*}\sqrt{2\log n}\quad\text{w.h.p.} $$

as $n\to\infty$ . The significance of this result is that in many examples, the second term in (1.5) matches the trivial lower bound $\|X\|\geq\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|$ ; this is the case, for example, for the random band matrix of Example 1.2. In such situations, (1.5) captures the exact leading order behavior $\|X\|=(1+o(1))\sigma_{*}\sqrt{2\log n}$ in the sparse regime $\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}\ll\sigma_{*}\sqrt{\log n}$ , while (1.3) necessarily loses a universal constant.

#### 1.1.3. Extremum principle

The proofs of Theorems 1.4 and 1.6 are based on a more fundamental principle that is of independent interest.

To explain this principle, let us begin by recalling the idea behind the proof of Theorem 1.1. Rather than bound the norm of the nonhomogeneous model $X$ directly, the approach of [4] compares $X$ with an i.i.d. matrix of smaller dimension, whose norm can be controlled by any classical method for homogeneous random matrices. In particular, the main technical device in [4] shows that when normalized so that $\sigma_{*}=1$ , the $2p$ -moment of $X$ can be bounded by the $2p$ -moment of a matrix with i.i.d. entries of dimension $\lceil\sigma_{1}^{2}+p\rceil\times\lceil\sigma_{2}^{2}+p\rceil$ . This suffices to capture the leading order behavior of $\|X\|$ , but the dependence of the comparison matrix on $p$ precludes any accurate control of the fluctuations.

The basis for the results of this paper may be viewed as an optimal comparison principle of this kind. In the following, we denote by $\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M$ the (unnormalized) trace and by $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}M:=\frac{1}{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M$ the normalized trace of an $n\times n$ matrix $M$ .

#### Theorem 1.7 (Extremum principle).

Let $X$ be as in Model 1.3 with $\sigma_{*}=1$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(XX^{*})^{p}]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(YY^{*})^{p}]\quad\text{for all }p\in\mathbb{N}, $$

where $Y$ is the $\lceil\sigma_{1}^{2}\rceil\times\lceil\sigma_{2}^{2}\rceil$ matrix with independent entries $Y_{ij}\sim N(0,1)$ .

Note that the inequality in Theorem 1.7 holds with equality when $X$ has i.i.d. entries. Thus, in contrast to the comparison principle of [4], Theorem 1.7 may be viewed as an extremum principle for random matrices. In terms of normalized moments, this principle may be expressed as follows.

#### Corollary 1.8.

Fix $d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{N}$ . Among all $X$ as in Model 1.3 with $\sigma_{*}^{2}=1$ , $\sigma_{1}^{2}\leq d_{1}$ , $\sigma_{2}^{2}\leq d_{2}$ , and arbitrary dimensions $n\times m$ , the normalized moments $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(XX^{*})^{p}]$ are maximized for all $p$ by the matrix of dimension $d_{1}\times d_{2}$ with i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ entries.

In terms of unnormalized moments, we obtain the following.

#### Corollary 1.9.

Fix $n,m,d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\frac{m}{d_{2}}\geq\frac{n}{d_{1}}\in\mathbb{N}$ . Among all $X$ as in Model 1.3 with $\sigma_{*}^{2}=1$ , $\sigma_{1}^{2}\leq d_{1}$ , $\sigma_{2}^{2}\leq d_{2}$ , and fixed dimensions $n\times m$ , the unnormalized moments $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}(XX^{*})^{p}]$ are maximized for all $p$ by the block-diagonal matrix whose blocks have dimension $d_{1}\times d_{2}$ and i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ entries (Figure 1.1).

*Figure 1.1. An extremal block-diagonal matrix.*

In particular, that block-diagonal matrices have the largest moments explains the form of Theorem 1.4. Indeed, as the norm of a block-diagonal matrix is the maximum of the norms of its blocks, (1.1) suggests that its distribution is approximately the maximum of $\frac{n}{d_{1}}$ independent Tracy-Widom variables. The tail probabilities of this distribution are precisely of the form that is captured by the tail bound of Theorem 1.4. In particular, the bound (1.4) is essentially the best possible in that it yields the correct behavior of block-diagonal matrices.

Theorem 1.7 will be proved in section 4 below. With this result in hand, the proof of Theorems 1.4 and 1.6 will reduce to the proof of analogous tail bounds for Wishart matrices. The latter is made possible by a beautiful method, pioneered by Ledoux [15, 16, 17], for deriving Tracy-Widom type tail bounds from sharp moment estimates.11 1 Tail bounds for Wigner and Wishart matrices have also been proved by methods that are not based on moments, such as in [1, 18]. However, as Theorem 1.7 only provides a comparison principle for moments and not for tail probabilities, the moment approach is essential here. While such estimates were obtained by Ledoux for GUE [15] and GOE [17] matrices, sharp moment bounds for Wishart matrices do not appear to be known in the literature. Such bounds are obtained here in section 5. The Wishart model is considerably more delicate than the GUE and GOE models due to the fact that we require bounds that hold uniformly for all dimensions $n,m$ , not just in the asymptotic regime (1.1) where $m=cn$ are proportional.

Let us emphasize that, despite the apparent similarity between Theorem 1.7 and the comparison principles of [4], the proofs of these results are completely different. The method of [4] uses a classical combinatorial expression for the moments as a sum over equivalence classes of even closed walks, and estimates each term separately. In contrast, the proof of Theorem 1.7 expresses the moments of a Gaussian random matrix as a sum over pairings by the Wick formula, and then uses an iterative procedure to reduce each term to a noncrossing pairing. This new approach turns out to provide a much more efficient mechanism for controlling the moments.

#### 1.1.4. Self-adjoint models and outline

While we have focused the discussion in the introduction on non-self-adjoint models for concreteness, analogous results hold also for self-adjoint models. Beside that self-adjoint random matrices arise frequently in applications, the proofs of the self-adjoint analogues of our main results turn out to be simpler than those in the non-self-adjoint case. We will therefore develop these results in detail before we return to the non-self-adjoint case.

- $\bullet$ In section 2 we consider self-adjoint random matrices with independent complex Gaussian entries. The extremum principle admits a particularly simple proof in this setting that avoids almost all the complications that arise in the real case.

- $\bullet$ We then consider in section 3 self-adjoint random matrices with independent real entries, that is, the self-adjoint analogue of Model 1.3. The proof of the the extremum principle is much more involved in this case, and shares the same difficulties as the proof of the extremum principle for non-self-adjoint models. However, for both complex and real self-adjoint models, we can directly invoke the moment estimates of Ledoux [15, 16, 17] to obtain tail bounds.

- $\bullet$ Finally, the non-self-adjoint case is developed in section 4, while section 5 developes the sharp moment estimates that are needed in this case.

### 1.2. Discussion and open questions

#### 1.2.1. Intrinsic freeness

To date, two main approaches have been developed for obtaining sharp nonasymptotic bounds for the spectral norm of nonhomogeneous random matrices $X$ that are of a fundamentally different nature:

- 1. The extremum principles of [4] and of this paper compare the spectral statistics of $X$ with those of an i.i.d. random matrix $Y$ of smaller dimension.

- 2. The intrinsic freeness principle of [2] compares the spectral statistics of $X$ with those of a deterministic operator $X_{\rm free}$ that arises in free probability theory.

The theory of [2] is in fact much more general than the setting of this paper, in that it captures both random matrices with dependent entries and more general spectral statistics. However, the following special case may be directly compared to the bounds of this paper: if $X$ is an $n\times m$ random matrix with independent Gaussian entries $X_{ij}\sim N(0,b_{ij}^{2})$ and $n\leq m$ , then [2, Corollary 2.2] yields

$$ \|X\|\leq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm free}\|+C_{\varepsilon}\,\sigma_{*}(\log m)^{3/2}\quad\text{w.h.p.} $$

for every $\varepsilon>0$ (this may be shown as in [2, Lemma 3.1]). As

$$ \|X_{\rm free}\|\leq\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2} $$

by [2, Lemma 2.5], the intrinsic freeness principle readily yields a slightly weaker form of (1.3). Note that the second term in (1.6) is even larger than that of (1.3), while the results of this paper yield a much smaller second-order term.

On the other hand, there are many situations where the intrinsic freeness principle yields strictly better results than those of this paper: whenever

$$ \sigma_{*}(\log m)^{3/2}\ll\|X_{\rm free}\|\leq(1-\delta)(\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}) $$

for some $\delta>0$ , the bound of (1.6) is strictly better to leading order, which renders any improvement to the second-order term negligible.

In view of the above discussion, the bounds of this paper are of particular interest when $\|X_{\rm free}\|=\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}$ . The following lemma explains when this is the case.

#### Lemma 1.10.

$\|X_{\rm free}\|=\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}$ when $\sum_{i}b_{ij}^{2}=\sigma_{1}^{2}$ and $\sum_{j}b_{ij}^{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}$ for all $i,j$ .

#### Proof.

We can apply [2, Lemma 3.2 and Remark 2.6] to obtain

$$ \|X_{\rm free}\|\geq 2\sum_{i}\sqrt{w_{i}\sum_{j}b_{ij}^{2}v_{j}}+2\sum_{j}\sqrt{w_{i}\sum_{i}b_{ij}^{2}v_{j}} $$

for every $w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , $v\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+}$ with $\sum_{i}w_{i}+\sum_{j}v_{j}=1$ . The conclusion follows by choosing $w_{i}=\frac{1}{2n}$ , $v_{j}=\frac{1}{2m}$ , and noting that $\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}^{2}=m\sigma_{1}^{2}=n\sigma_{2}^{2}$ . ∎

Variance patterns with constant row and column sums as in Lemma 1.10 arise naturally in applications, for example, in the study of sparse random matrices whose sparsity pattern is biregular. At the same time, the results of this paper are stronger than those obtained by the intrinsic freeness principle for very sparse matrices (so that they capture phase transitions as in Example 1.2), and provide the strongest easily computable norm bounds for arbitrary variance patterns.

One may wonder whether it might in fact be possible to achieve the best of both worlds: could the tail bound of Theorem 1.4 with fluctuations at Tracy-Widom scale remain valid if the leading term $\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}$ is replaced by $\|X_{\rm free}\|$ ? The following example shows that such a bound cannot exist.

#### Example 1.11.

Let $n=m$ and $b_{ij}^{2}=n^{-1}(1+\delta^{2}1_{i=1})$ , known as the spiked covariance model (originally due to Baik, Ben Arous, and Péché in the complex case). Then the leading order behavior of $\|X\|$ exhibits the following phase transition:

$$ \|X\|=(1+o(1))\|X_{\rm free}\|=(1+o(1))\begin{cases}2&\text{if }\delta\leq 1,\\
\delta+\frac{1}{\delta}&\text{if }\delta>1\end{cases}\qquad\text{w.h.p.} $$

as $n\to\infty$ (cf. [2, 3] and [21, §2.1]). Moreover, it is shown in [21, Theorem 3] that when $\delta>1$ , the fluctuations of $\|X\|$ are of order $\sigma_{*}\sim n^{-1/2}$ . This shows that we cannot replace $\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}$ by $\|X_{\rm free}\|$ in Theorem 1.4, as that would imply a much smaller bound on the fluctuations of order $\sigma_{*}^{4/3}$ .

Example 1.11 illustrates in a particularly clear manner that the extremum and intrinsic freeness principles capture fundamentally different mathematical phenomena. This may appear somewhat surprising, given that both the proofs in this paper and those of [2] are based on the control of crossings in the Wick formula (in the latter case, this idea is due to [24]). However, these results exploit crossings in very different ways: here we show that the contribution of each crossing to the nonhomogeneous model is bounded by that in the i.i.d. model, while the intrinsic freeness principle aims to show that crossings are negligible altogether.

#### 1.2.2. Superconcentration

The concentration of measure phenomenon [14] is a powerful tool for bounding the fluctuations of random structures. While general concentration inequalities often yield optimal bounds, there are also situations where the scale of the flucutations is much smaller than is predicted by general principles. This phenomenon was called superconcentration in [7].

When applied to the random matrix models of this paper, classical concentration inequalities ensure that the scale of the fluctuations of $\|X\|$ is at most of order $\sigma_{*}$ , cf. [2, Corollary 4.14]. In contrast, the fluctuation term in Theorem 1.4, of order $\sigma_{*}^{4/3}\sigma_{1}^{-1/3}$ , is often much smaller than $\sigma_{*}$ . We may therefore think of Theorem 1.4 as a ‘‘matrix superconcentration inequality’’. Indeed, this bound accurately captures the well known superconcentration property of the upper tail of the norm of Wishart matrices, and extends it to a much larger class of models.22 2 After the completion of this paper, we learned that a weaker superconcentration property was previously obtained by entirely different methods in [10, Theorem 3.4] for self-adjoint random matrices satisfying the analogue of Lemma 1.10. Theorem 3.4 below yields a much more precise tail bound in the self-adjoint setting that is essentially optimal by the extremum principle.

This interpretation must be treated with care, however, as the second-order term in Theorem 1.4 can only provide information on the fluctuations of $\|X\|$ when the first-order term is captured correctly. In particular, Theorem 1.4 can only establish genuine superconcentration for variance patterns that satisfy conditions as in Lemma 1.10. This is necessarily the case: Example 1.11 illustrates that general variance patterns may not exhibit any superconcentration at all.

More generally, it is not expected that the specific setting of Lemma 1.10 is necessary for superconcentration. General principles explained in [7] suggest that the spectral norm should exhibit superconcentration provided there are many singular values near the maximal one (this fails in Example 1.11, where the largest singular value is isolated from the bulk). Furthermore, even in the setting of Lemma 1.10, our results yield an upper bound that is sharp for block-diagonal matrices, but other such models may exhibit even smaller fluctuations (e.g., [23]). A precise understanding of when and how much superconcentration arises for nonhomogeneous random matrices remains out of reach of any known method.

#### 1.2.3. Universality

The setting of Model 1.3 requires the entries of $X$ to be symmetrically distributed and have all their moments dominated by those of the Gaussian distribution. However, the classical Tracy-Widom asymptotics (1.1) remain valid in a much more general setting [22]: it suffices that the entries of $X$ have zero mean, unit variance, and soft control of the higher moments.

It is of considerable interest to understand whether nonasymptotic bounds can also be achieved in this much more general setting. An extension of Theorem 1.1 along these lines was proved in [13, §4.3]: it was shown there that for any random matrix $X$ whose entries are independent and have zero mean, the statement of Theorem 1.1 remains valid if we replace the parameters (1.2) by

$$ \sigma_{1}^{2}\leftarrow\max_{j}\sum_{i}\mathrm{Var}(X_{ij}),\qquad\sigma_{2}^{2}\leftarrow\max_{i}\sum_{j}\mathrm{Var}(X_{ij}),\qquad\sigma_{*}^{2}\leftarrow\max_{i,j}\|X_{ij}\|_{\infty}^{2}. $$

However, just as Theorem 1.1, this result fails to capture fluctuations at the Tracy-Widom scale. It is natural to conjecture the validity of an analogous extension of Theorem 1.4 and of the other main results of this paper. Such results would be of particular interest in applications, e.g., to random graphs [5].

Unfortunately, it is not clear whether the methods of this paper can be adapted to achieve such results (nor do they follow from the very general universality principles in [6], whose error terms are far larger than the fluctuations in Theorem 1.4). While much less precise, the method used in [4, 13] does not use any special properties of the Gaussian distribution and is therefore readily adapted to more general models. In contrast, the proof of the sharp extremum principle of Theorem 1.7 is based on the Wick formula, and is therefore inherently Gaussian in nature. For this reason, an analogous extension of our main results remains an open problem.

### 1.3. Notation

The following notation will be used throughout this paper.

We denote by $N(0,\sigma^{2})$ or by $N_{\mathbb{R}}(0,\sigma^{2})$ the distribution of a real Gaussian random variable with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ . The distribution of a complex random variable, whose real and imaginary parts are independent with distribution $N_{\mathbb{R}}(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2})$ (i.e., a complex Gaussian variable), is denoted as $N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,\sigma^{2})$ .

For a matrix $M$ , its adjoint is denoted as $M^{*}$ ; in particular, $a^{*}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $a\in\mathbb{C}$ . We always denote by $\|M\|$ the spectral norm (i.e., the largest singular value) of $M$ . Recall that for a square matrix $M$ , we denote by $\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M$ and $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}M$ the unnormalized and normalized trace, respectively.

We write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . We denote by $\mathrm{P}_{2}([n])$ the set of all pairings of $[n]$ (that is, partitions each of whose elements has size two). Recall that given any $\pi\in\mathrm{P}_{2}([n])$ , two pairs $\{i,k\},\{j,l\}\in\pi$ such that $i<j<k<l$ are said to form a crossing. A pairing that contains no crossing is said to be noncrossing, and we denote by $\mathrm{NC}_{2}([n])$ the set of all noncrossing pairings of $[n]$ .

Finally, we will write $x\lesssim y$ to indicate that $x\leq Cy$ for a universal constant $C$ .

## 2. The Hermitian case

The aim of this section is to investigate Hermitian random matrices with independent complex Gaussian entries. That is, we consider the following model.

#### Model 2.1.

$X$ is an $n\times n$ Hermitian matrix whose entries $X_{ij}=(X_{ji})^{*}$ are independent for $i\geq j$ with $X_{ij}\sim N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,b_{ij}^{2})$ for $i>j$ and $X_{ii}\sim N_{\mathbb{R}}(0,b_{ii}^{2})$ , where $b_{ij}=b_{ji}\geq 0$ are arbitrary nonnegative scalars.

This setting admits particularly simple proofs, which will guide the more involved arguments required for real random matrices in the following sections.

Define the parameters

$$ \sigma^{2}:=\max_{i\leq n}\sum_{j\leq n}b_{ij}^{2},\qquad\qquad\sigma_{*}^{2}:=\max_{i,j\leq n}b_{ij}^{2}. $$

Then we have the following extremum principle and tail bounds.

#### Theorem 2.2 (Extremum principle).

Define $X$ as in Model 2.1, and assume that $\sigma_{*}^{2}=1$ and that $\sigma^{2}\leq d\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then we have

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2p}]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Y^{2p}] $$

for all $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , where $Y$ is the $d\times d$ Hermitian matrix whose entries $Y_{ij}=(Y_{ji})^{*}$ are independent for $i\geq j$ with $Y_{ij}\sim N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1)$ for $i>j$ and $Y_{ii}\sim N_{\mathbb{R}}(0,1)$ .

#### Theorem 2.3 (Small deviations).

For $X$ as in Model 2.1, we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>2\sigma+4\sigma_{*}^{4/3}\sigma^{-1/3}t\big]\leq\frac{en\sigma_{*}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}e^{-t^{3/2}} $$

for every $0\leq t\leq\frac{\sigma^{4/3}}{\sigma_{*}^{4/3}}$ .

#### Theorem 2.4 (Large deviations).

For $X$ as in Model 2.1, we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X\|>2\sigma+\sigma_{*}(1+t)\big]\leq 2n\,e^{-t^{2}/2} $$

for every $t\geq 0$ .

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proofs of these results.

### 2.1. Extremum principle

In this subsection, we will use the following notation. Let $(g_{ij})_{i\geq j}$ be i.i.d. $N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1)$ random variables, and define

$$ U_{ij}:=b_{ij}e_{i}e_{j}^{*},\qquad\qquad U_{ii}:=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}b_{ii}e_{i}e_{i}^{*} $$

for $i>j$ . Then we can represent the random matrix $X$ of Model 2.1 as

$$ X=\sum_{i\geq j}(g_{ij}U_{ij}+g_{ij}^{*}U_{ij}^{*}). $$

We can compute the moments of $X$ as follows.

#### Lemma 2.5 (Wick formula).

For any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2p}]=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}_{2}([2p])}\sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}. $$

Here $\bm{i}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{2p})\in[n]^{2p}$ , $\bm{j}=(j_{1},\ldots,j_{2p})\in[n]^{2p}$ , $\bm{\varepsilon}=(\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{2p})\in\{1,*\}^{2p}$ , and $(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi$ denotes $i_{k}\geq j_{k}$ and $i_{k}=i_{l},j_{k}=j_{l},\varepsilon_{k}\neq\varepsilon_{l}$ for all $\{k,l\}\in\pi$ .

#### Proof.

Clearly

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2p}]=\sum_{i_{1}\geq j_{1},\ldots,i_{2p}\geq j_{2p}}\sum_{\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{2p}\in\{1,*\}}\mathbf{E}[g_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots g_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}]\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}. $$

The conclusion follows as

$$ \mathbf{E}[g_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots g_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}]=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}_{2}([2p])}\prod_{\{k,l\}\in\pi}1_{i_{k}=i_{l},j_{k}=j_{l},\varepsilon_{k}\neq\varepsilon_{l}} $$

by the classical Wick formula [20, Theorem 22.3 and Remark 22.5]. ∎

Free probability theory suggests [20, p. 367] that the expression in Lemma 2.5 should be dominated by noncrossing pairings. The idea behind the proof of Theorem 2.2 is to consider separately the effect of noncrossing and crossing pairs on the terms in the sum in Lemma 2.5. We first consider noncrossing pairings.

#### Lemma 2.6.

For any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ and noncrossing pairing $\pi\in\mathrm{NC}_{2}([2p])$ , we have

$$ \sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}\leq\sigma^{2p}. $$

Moreover, equality holds when $b_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$ .

#### Proof.

Recall the elementary fact that any noncrossing pairing $\pi$ must contain a consecutive pair $\{k,k+1\}\in\pi$ . (If not, choose $\{k,k+l\}\in\pi$ with minimal $l\geq 2$ . Then $\{k+1,r\}\in\pi$ must satisfy $|k+1-r|\geq l$ . In particular, $\{k,k+l\}$ and $\{k+1,r\}$ form a crossing, contradicting the assumption.)

By cyclic permutation of the trace, we may assume without loss of generality that $\{2p-1,2p\}\in\pi$ . Then we can compute

$$ \sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}=\\
\sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi\backslash\{\{2p-1,2p\}\}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p-2}j_{2p-2}}^{\varepsilon_{2p-2}}\sum_{i\geq j}(U_{ij}U_{ij}^{*}+U_{ij}^{*}U_{ij}). $$

Now note that

$$ \sum_{i\geq j}(U_{ij}U_{ij}^{*}+U_{ij}^{*}U_{ij})=\sum_{i\leq n}\bigg(\sum_{j\leq n}b_{ij}^{2}\bigg)e_{i}e_{i}^{*}. $$

As all $U_{ij}$ have nonnegative entries, we have $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p-2}j_{2p-2}}^{\varepsilon_{2p-2}}e_{i}e_{i}^{*}\geq 0$ . Thus

$$ \sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p}j_{2p}}^{\varepsilon_{2p}}\leq\sigma^{2}\sum_{(\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{\varepsilon})\sim\pi\backslash\{\{2p-1,2p\}\}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}U_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots U_{i_{2p-2}j_{2p-2}}^{\varepsilon_{2p-2}}, $$

with equality if $b_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$ . As $\pi\backslash\{\{2p-1,2p\}\}$ is again a noncrossing pairing, we can iterate this argument to conclude the proof. ∎

Next, we analyze the effect of a single crossing.

#### Lemma 2.7 (Crossing inequality).

Let $M_{1},\ldots,M_{4}$ be any $n\times n$ matrices with nonnegative entries. Then we have
