$$ \|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\left(n\frac{\tau}{d}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\log^{9}n+\log^{4}n. $$

Noticing that $\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\log^{9}(n)\geq\log^{4}n$ and $np\tau^{2}\log^{9}n\geq np\tau^{2}\log^{4}n$ , gives the statement of the Proposition.∎

## 7. Generalization to Numerically Low-Rank Data

In this section we prove Theorem 2.5, which relaxes the strict rank assumption of Theorem 4.1. The general approach is to pass to a low-rank projection of the data matrix $X$ . Hence, the statements and proofs of many lemmas and propositions mirror those of Theorem 4.1, but additional arguments are needed to handle errors arising from the spectral projection.

Recall our notation $\Pi^{(k)}_{M}$ for the matrix for projection to the span of the top $k$ eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix $M$ . Write $X_{k}:=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}X$ , and set

$$ \tilde{Y}:=X_{k}+Z,\qquad\tilde{A}_{ij}:=\1\!\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right), $$

so that $\tilde{Y}$ is the noisy version of the spectrally truncated point cloud $X_{k}$ and $\tilde{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the exactly-rank- $k$ model on $\tilde{Y}$ , whose rows are $\tilde{y}_{i}=\tilde{x}_{i}+z_{i}$ . Set $X_{k+1:d}:=X-X_{k}$ , and, recalling $\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X$ , set

$$ \Sigma_{k}:=\frac{1}{n}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}X_{k}\,,\qquad\Sigma_{k+1:d}:=\Sigma-\Sigma_{k}=\frac{1}{n}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}X_{k+1:d}. $$

The spectral embedding $X_{G}$ is, as before, built from the top- $k$ eigenpairs of the observed matrix $A$ . Note that Lemma 4.2 was already stated under the assumptions of Theorem 2.5, so we can carry on the rest of the proof with $\hat{X}$ in place of $X_{G}$ .

The proof proceeds in three main steps, summarized as follows.

- (i) Parameter truncation: Under (2.7) the truncation does not change the leading order model parameters: $\Tr\Sigma=(1+o(1))\Tr\Sigma_{k}$ , the threshold $\tau$ and first Gegenbauer coefficient $p_{1}$ are unchanged to leading order, and $p=(1+o(1))\tilde{p}$ by Lemma 7.9. Consequently every parameter estimate proved for the truncated model (Appendix A) transfers verbatim, up to $(1+o(1))$ factors, to the observed model. In fact, the parameter estimate proofs in the appendix are done for this generalized case.

- (ii) One further projection: We pick up an additional error term in passing from the full-rank projected data $Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}$ to the truncated projected data $\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}$ , defined as $\tilde{Y}_{k}=\Pi_{\tilde{Y}}^{(k)}\tilde{Y}$ . This step is spelled out in (7.2).

- (iii) One new comparison: Because $\hat{X}$ is built from the observed adjacency matrix $A$ , while the rank- $k$ truncated data describes $\tilde{A}$ , the comparison step of Theorem 4.1 picks up an additional summand $\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . This new term is the source of the truncation term in (2.8).

We bound

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

The second term is new and is controlled by concentration arguments – see Lemma 7.3. To bound the third term we now use the truncated adjacency matrix $\tilde{A}$ , and the data matrix is redefined as $\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+p_{1}d_{k}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ . Then to pass to the observed adjacency matrix $A$ we need to estimate $\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . For additional clarity, Figure 5 is a diagram that illustrates the new steps, incorporated within the proof of the strictly rank– $k$ case.

*Figure 5. Structure of the proof of Theorem 2.5. Steps for the argument for Theorem 4.1 (strict rank- $k$ case) are shaded blue. For numerically low-rank data, two new components are added in red: the additional triangle inequality term passing from the full-rank projected data to the truncated projected data, and, inside the proof of Proposition 7.5, a step estimating $\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ .*

### 7.1. Projection and Perturbation Step Analogues

We begin by stating an extension of Lemma 5.3.

#### Lemma 7.1.

With probability at least $1-e^{-\sqrt{d}}$ , $\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})\leq\frac{n}{d}+O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}+\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2}\Big)$ . The estimates of $\lambda_{i}(YY^{\mathsf{T}}),1\leq i\leq k$ agree with Lemma 5.3.

#### Proof.

The proof follows the Cauchy Interlacing part of the proof of (5.3), specifically the decomposition (6.1), but adding the “leftover” coordinates to the lower-right block of the matrix 5.11. ∎

#### Lemma 7.2 (Clean Data and Noisy Data Projection Matrix Distance Generalized).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ ,

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is analogous to Lemma 5.1, except for the first triangle inequality which separates the trailing eigenvalues of $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ from the first $k$ .

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|X_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+(\|X_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}})\|X_{k}-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

The first term on the right hand side of (7.3) is $n\mu_{k+1}^{2}$ . For the second summand on the right hand side, we have that with probability at least $1-e^{-d}$ ,

$$ \|X_{k}-Y_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\|X_{k}-Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=2\|X_{k}-(X+Z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2(\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}})\lesssim\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}. $$

Then, combining (7.3) and (7.4) with bounds from the proof of Lemma 5.1 yields

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+n\mu_{1}(\mu_{k+1}+1/\sqrt{d}). $$

From the conditions (2.7) it follows $\mu_{k+1}\leq d^{-1/2}\leq\mu_{k}\leq\mu_{1}$ , so the right hand side is $O(n\mu_{1}/\sqrt{d})$ as claimed. ∎

#### Lemma 7.3 (Original and Truncated Data Difference).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, we have with probability at least $1-e^{-\sqrt{d}}$ ,

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\mu_{k+1}. $$

#### Proof.

Recall that $\tilde{Y}_{k}=\Pi_{\tilde{Y}}^{(k)}(X_{k}+Z),Y_{k}=\Pi_{Y}^{(k)}(X+Z)$ , for short, we will use $\Pi=\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}$ as in the proof of Lemma 5.2 and $\tilde{\Pi}=\Pi^{(k)}_{\tilde{Y}}$ Using the triangle inequality, we introduce an intermediate term $\Pi^{(k)}_{Y}\tilde{Y}=\Pi\tilde{Y}$ :

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} $$

Then, estimating the first term on the right hand side via concentration of the operator norm of $Z$ (e.g. [28, Theorem 4.4.5]) yields, that with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\left\|\Pi\left[X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}+(X_{k}-X)Z^{\mathsf{T}}+Z(X_{k}-X)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]\Pi\right\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}+(X_{k}-X)Z^{\mathsf{T}}+Z(X_{k}-X)^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|X-X_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}^{2}+n\mu_{k+1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\mu_{k+1} $$

where we used (5.9) in the final line. As for the second expression in (7.6), we write

$$ \displaystyle\|\Pi\tilde{Y}(\Pi\tilde{Y})^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\|(\Pi-\tilde{\Pi})\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\tilde{\Pi}+\Pi\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}(\Pi-\tilde{\Pi})\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|\Pi-\tilde{\Pi}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})}\quad\text{ by \lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{DavisKahanForProjections}}. $$

By definition of $\tilde{Y}$ , we know that $\lambda_{1}(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}})=n\mu_{1}^{2}=\lambda_{1}(XX^{\mathsf{T}})$ , so by the same argument as Lemma 5.3, $\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=n\mu_{1}^{2}+O(n/d)\lesssim n\mu_{1}^{2},$ with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ , and similarly combining Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 7.1 gives us an estimate on the eigenvalue gap

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{k}(YY^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(YY^{\mathsf{T}}) \displaystyle\geq n\mu_{k}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}-O\left(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1}d^{-1/4}\right)-\bigg(\frac{n}{d}+O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}+\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2}\Big)\bigg) \displaystyle\gtrsim n\mu_{k}^{2}. $$

In the last line, we use (2.7), (2.5) and $d<n$ to obtain the dominant term. Then, by the same lines as in (7.7), we have that with probability $1-O(e^{-d})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim n\mu_{k+1}/\sqrt{d}\,. $$

Plugging these estimates into (7.8), then adding to (7.7) gives us:

$$ \|Y_{k}Y_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\mu_{k+1}+n\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}(\mu_{k+1}^{2}+\mu_{k+1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}})\lesssim\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\frac{n\mu_{k+1}}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

as claimed. ∎

#### Lemma 7.4 (Embedding Matrix and Noisy Data Projection Matrix Difference).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, we have with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ ,

$$ \|\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}_{k}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{\mu_{k}^{2}}\big\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 7.4.

The argument coincides with that of Lemma 5.2 up to the final substitution, so we only indicate the changes. Let us use the following shorthand notation, to avoid clutter: $\tilde{Y}=X_{k}+Z$ is the truncated noisy data, and we abbreviate $\tilde{\Pi}=\Pi^{(k)}_{\tilde{Y}}$ and $\hat{\Pi}=\Pi^{(k)}_{\hat{Y}}$ for the projections onto the top $k$ eigenvectors of $\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ respectively.

The projection decomposition (5.16) and the term-by-term estimates $(i)$ – $(iii)$ hold verbatim with $\tilde{Y},\tilde{\Pi}$ in place of $Y,\Pi$ . Terms $(i)$ – $(ii)$ are controlled through Davis–Kahan (Lemma 5.4) and $(iii)$ directly, yielding

$$ \|\tilde{Y}_{k}\tilde{Y}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\left(\frac{\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})}+1\right). $$

$\tilde{Y}=X_{k}+Z$ has rank- $k$ signal, thus the eigenvalue estimates of Equation 5.3 apply verbatim to $\tilde{Y}$ , the spectral gap is then $\lambda_{k}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})-\lambda_{k+1}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})\gtrsim n\mu_{k}^{2}$ . Substituting then gives Lemma 7.4. ∎

We have the following analogue of Proposition 4.4:

#### Proposition 7.5.

Under the conditions of Theorem 2.5, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10}$ ),

$$ \big\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\sqrt{d}\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr(\Sigma)\log^{4}(n)+\left(n\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{d^{3/2}}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{dp}}\right)\log^{9}n+\frac{n}{dp\tau}\left(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\right)^{1/4}. $$

We defer the proof of this Proposition to Section 7.2.

Now that we have all the components from (7.2), we can complete the proof of the theorem.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.5.

The passage from $X_{G}$ to $\hat{X}$ follows from the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 4.1 using Lemma 4.2. The proof is concluded by combining Lemmas 7.2, 7.3, 7.4 and Proposition 7.5 with (7.2). ∎

### 7.2. Comparison Step

Recall that in the proof of Theorem 2.5, we used Proposition 7.5, a quantitative control on $\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . In this subsection we explain how Proposition 7.5 follows from combining the arguments of Section 6 (replacing occurrences of $Y$ with $\tilde{Y}$ ) with a good enough quantitative bound on $\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ (see Proposition 7.6).

#### 7.2.1. Truncating the Adjacency Matrix

In this section, we will show that the observed adjacency matrix $A_{ij}=\1\left(y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)$ is well-approximated by adjacency matrix $\tilde{A}=\1\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)$ , induced by the strictly low-rank data. This is the first component that we need to find to prove Proposition 7.5.

#### Proposition 7.6 (Truncation Error).

Under the same assumptions as Theorem 2.5, and $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}>0$ (otherwise we reduce to the strictly rank $-k$ case, as we have already done in Theorem 4.1). Then, with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim n\left(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\right)^{1/4}+\log n. $$

To prove this proposition, we first define a continuous approximation to the indicator function. For $\delta>0$ , let:

$$ I_{\delta}(x)=\begin{cases}0\quad&\text{ if }x<\tau-\delta,\\
\frac{1}{\delta}(x-\tau+\delta)\quad&\text{ if }\tau-\delta\leq x<\tau,\\
1\quad&\text{ if }x\geq\tau.\end{cases} $$

Note that $I_{\delta}$ is $(1/\delta)$ -Lipschitz and bounded between 0 and 1. Let $A_{\delta},\tilde{A}_{\delta}$ be matrices with entries $I_{\delta}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle)$ , $I_{\delta}(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle)$ , respectively, where we recall that $\tilde{y}_{i}=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}x_{i}+z_{i}$ . We split the error as follows:

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|A-A_{\delta}+\tilde{A}_{\delta}-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

#### Lemma 7.7 (Lipschitz Approximation Error).

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ :

$$ \|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\delta\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/2}\qquad\forall\delta>0. $$

#### Proof.

We will use the Frobenius norm to control the operator norm since $\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{F}$ . Then, explicitly writing out the component-wise difference, we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle|I_{\delta}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle)-I_{\delta}(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle)| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\delta}|\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle-\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle|=:\frac{1}{\delta}M_{ij}, $$

and thus $\|A_{\delta}-\tilde{A}_{\delta}\|_{F}\leq\frac{1}{\delta}\|M\|_{F}$ . We can express the matrix $M$ as a function of the noise vectors $M=M(Z)=\frac{1}{\delta}\left(X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}+X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}+ZX_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\right)$ , where $Z$ contains the noise vectors as rows and $X_{k+1:d}=X-X_{k}=(I-\Pi^{(k)}_{X})X$ is the projection onto the tail eigenspace.

Note that for different inputs $W,W^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , the reverse triangle inequality and the non-commutative Hölder inequality yield:

$$ \displaystyle\big|\|M(W)\|_{F}-\|M(W^{\prime})\|_{F}\big| \displaystyle\leq\|M(W)-M(W^{\prime})\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|X_{k+1:d}(W-W^{\prime})^{\mathsf{T}}+(W-W^{\prime})X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}\|W-W^{\prime}\|_{F}. $$

Therefore $\|M(Z)\|_{F}$ is a $2\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}$ -Lipschitz function (with respect to the Euclidean Frobenius metric) of Gaussian noise with variance $\frac{1}{d}$ . From Gaussian concentration (see [28, Theorem 5.2.3 ]) it follows

$$ \mathbb{P}(\|M\|_{F}-\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F}\geq t)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{ct^{2}d}{n\mu^{2}_{k+1}}\right) $$

for any $t>0$ . Moreover, it is straightforward to control the expectation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}+2\mathbb{E}\|X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\bigg(\sqrt{n}\mu_{k+1}+2\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}\bigg)\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\sqrt{\sum_{l>k}\mu_{l}^{2}}. $$

The lemma follows by setting $t=C\sqrt{n/d}\mu_{k+1}\log n$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ , and noting that $\mu_{k+1}\log n\leq\sqrt{n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}$ . ∎

Now, we want to control the other part of the triangle inequality in (7.12), which captures the discontinuity of the hard indicator. Let $g(x)=\1(x\geq\tau)-I_{\delta}(x)$ , $Q_{ij}=\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle$ , and $\tilde{Q}_{ij}=\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle$ . Let $H$ be the symmetric matrix with entries $(A-A_{\delta}+\tilde{A}_{\delta}-\tilde{A})_{ij}=g(Q_{ij})-g(\tilde{Q}_{ij})$ . By the Schur test,

$$ \|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|H_{ij}| $$

Note that $0\leq|g(x)|\leq\1(x\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ . Thus, with $D_{ij}:=\1(Q_{ij}\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ and $\tilde{D}_{ij}:=\1(\tilde{Q}_{ij}\in[\tau-\delta,\tau])$ , we have

$$ |H_{ij}|\leq 2(D_{ij}+\tilde{D}_{ij})\qquad\forall i,j\in[n]. $$

#### Claim 7.8.

For any $\delta>0$ , with probability $1-O(e^{-cd})+O(ne^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n})$ ,

$$ \max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}\lesssim\delta\sqrt{d}n\,. $$

The same holds with $\tilde{D}$ in place of $D$ .

We first conclude the proof of Proposition 7.6 on the claim.

#### Proof of Proposition 7.6.

Let $\delta>0$ to be chosen. From (7.12), Lemma 7.7, (7.17) and Claim 7.8,

$$ \|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\frac{n}{\delta\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/2}+\delta\sqrt{d}n $$

with probability $1-O(n^{-10}+e^{-cd}+e^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n})$ . Taking $\delta=d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/4}+C\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}n}$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$ concludes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Claim 7.8.

We only give the argument for $D$ ; the argument for $\tilde{D}$ being almost identical.

Fixing an arbitrary $i\in[n]$ , note that conditional on $z_{i}$ , the $n-1$ variables $(Q_{ij})_{j\neq i}$ are independent and Gaussian, with $Q_{ij}$ having mean $\langle y_{i},x_{j}\rangle$ and variance $\|y_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/d$ . In particular, the conditional density of $Q_{ij}$ given $z_{i}$ is bounded by $O(\sqrt{d}/\|y_{i}\|_{2})$ . Letting $\mathcal{E}_{i}=\{\|y_{i}\|_{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\}$ , we have that on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ the variables $(D_{ij})_{j\neq i}$ are independent Bernoulli variables with expectations $O(\delta\sqrt{d})$ . From Bernstein’s inequality it follows $\1(\mathcal{E}_{i})\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}\lesssim\delta\sqrt{d}n$ with probability $1-O(\exp(-c\delta\sqrt{d}n))$ . Furthermore, we have $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i})\geq 1-e^{-cd}$ for all $i\in[n]$ . Indeed, from (2.6) we have $\|x_{i}\|_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma}=o(1)$ , while with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ , $\|z_{i}\|_{2}\in[\frac{1}{2},2]$ , and hence $\|y_{i}\|_{2}\geq\|z_{i}\|_{2}-\|x_{i}\|_{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}-o(1)$ . By the union bound, for $C$ sufficiently large we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}>C\delta\sqrt{d}n\bigg) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i}^{c})+\mathbb{P}\bigg(\1(\mathcal{E}_{i})\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{ij}>C\delta\sqrt{d}n\bigg) \displaystyle\lesssim n(e^{-cd}+e^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n}) \displaystyle\lesssim e^{-cd}+ne^{-c\delta\sqrt{d}n} $$

where in the last bound we used that $d=\omega(\log n)$ . ∎

In some of the parameter estimates for the truncated case we will approximate $p$ with $\tilde{p}$ , which we justify below.

#### 7.2.2. Estimation for Truncated Parameters

In this part of the subsection, we show that there is asymptotically (up to leading order) no difference between the parameters of $A$ and $\tilde{A}$ . We begin with $\tilde{p}$ :

#### Lemma 7.9.

Under the same conditions as Proposition 7.6, we have that

$$ (1+o(1))p=\tilde{p}. $$

#### Proof.

We use the same notation as in the proof of Proposition 7.6. We will use that for any $s>0$ ,

$$ |\1(Q_{ij}\geq\tau)-\1(\tilde{Q}_{ij}\geq\tau)|\leq\1[|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s]+\1[|Q_{ij}-\tau|<s]+\1[|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|<s]\,. $$

Fixing $s>0$ to be optimized later, we have

$$ \displaystyle|p-\tilde{p}| \displaystyle=\bigg|\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)-\mathbb{P}\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)\bigg| \displaystyle\leq\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big|\1\left(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)-\1\left(\langle\tilde{y}_{i},\tilde{y}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau\right)\big| \displaystyle\leq\binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tau|\leq s)+\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s)+\mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|<s)\qquad\text{by }\eqref{eqn: entrywise_p_tildep_UB}. $$

All that is left is to estimate the probabilities on the right hand side above. Recall from the proof of Claim 7.8 that

$$ \mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tau|\leq s),\mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Q}_{ij}-\tau|\leq s)\lesssim s\sqrt{d}+e^{-cd}. $$

Then, by Markov’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{P}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|\geq s) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{s^{2}}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}(|Q_{ij}-\tilde{Q}_{ij}|^{2})=\frac{1}{s^{2}}\sum_{i<j}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big(M_{ij}^{2}\big), $$

with $M=Q-\tilde{Q}=X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}+X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}+ZX_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}$ as in (7.14). We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|M\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|X_{k+1:d}Z^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{n}{d}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\leq(\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{n}{d})\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim\frac{n}{d}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2} $$

where in the final bound we used our assumption (2.7) that $\frac{1}{n}\|X_{k+1:d}\|_{F}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=o(1/d)$ . Combining with (7.20) yields

$$ |p-\tilde{p}|\lesssim s\sqrt{d}+e^{-cd}+\frac{1}{s^{2}d}\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\,. $$

Optimizing over $s$ gives $s=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/3}$ , which by plugging into the right hand side of our bound, and taking dominant terms yields

$$ |p-\tilde{p}|\lesssim(\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d})^{1/3}+e^{-cd}=o(p),\text{ by }\eqref{assu:gap-gen} $$

as desired.

∎

#### 7.2.3. Proof of Proposition 7.5

Recall that in Proposition 4.4, we controlled the quantity $\|YY^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by comparing the adjacency matrix to another matrix $B_{\text{data}}$ . To prove Proposition 7.5, we must instead control $\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ , we do this by comparing $\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ to the truncated versions of Definition 6.1,

$$ \boxed{\begin{aligned} \tilde{B}_{\text{data}}&=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\\
\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}}&=p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}+d_{k}p_{1}\Pi^{\perp}_{{\zeta}}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})\Pi^{\perp}_{{\zeta}}.\end{aligned}} $$

#### Proof of Proposition 7.5.

Recall that in this context $B_{\text{spec}}=\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}+d_{k}p_{1}\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is the rank– $d$ spectral decomposition of the observed adjacency matrix $A$ . Moreover, if $\tilde{A},\tilde{Y},\{\tilde{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\tilde{p}$ are the truncated analogues of $A,Y,\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},p$ , then Lemmas 6.10, 6.11 and 6.14 hold verbatim with these substitutions. In particular, note that $B_{\text{sph}}$ in (6.1), is now defined in terms of the decomposition of $\tilde{y}=(a_{i},w_{i})$ from (6.1).

Since $\{\tilde{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}=\{\Pi_{X}^{(k)}x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is exactly rank– $k$ , the noisy vectors $\tilde{y}_{i}=\tilde{x}_{i}+z_{i}$ satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 4.1 and the cited proofs depend on the signal only through the parameter estimates in Section 6.2, which remain unchanged after truncation due to Lemma 7.9 and $\tau$ remaining fixed; in particular, we note that coefficients $p_{i}$ in the Gegenbauer expansion $\1(x\geq\tau)=p_{0}+p_{1}x+\dots$ remain the same. Thus,

$$ \displaystyle d_{k}p_{1}\|\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|B_{\text{spec}}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|A-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq 2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+4\|\tilde{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \displaystyle\leq\left(2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\|\tilde{B}_{\text{sph}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-p_{0}\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right) \displaystyle\qquad+\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+4\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Note that the terms inside the parentheses can be controlled via Lemma 6.10, Lemma 6.11 and Lemma 6.14, which combined together give the conclusion of Proposition 4.4. We already have an estimate on $\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ , while $\|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ can be controlled via Davis–Kahan and Weyl’s inequality:

$$ \|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\rvert\eta_{0}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\lvert+\tilde{\eta}_{0}\|\mathbf{w}_{0}-\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\|_{2}\leq\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+2\tilde{\eta}_{0}\frac{\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A})}. $$

We estimate the spectral gap $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A})$ by first applying Weyl’s inequality to relate it to $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})$ . Next $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})$ can be estimated by following the argument in Section 6.4; to find the eigenvalues of $\tilde{B}_{\text{data}},$ we must project away from the first eigenspace, which is spanned by $\zeta$ . To this end, we apply Weyl’s inequality once again:

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A}) \displaystyle\geq\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{data}})-2\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\geq\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})-2(\|\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}). $$

By (6.28) , we have that $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})=\Theta(\tilde{p}n)=\Theta(pn)$ , where the last equality is given by Lemma 7.9. Moreover, the bounds from Lemmas 6.10, 6.11 and 6.15 give: $\|\tilde{A}-\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\tilde{B}_{\text{data}}-\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=o(pn)$ by (2.4), (2.5) and Lemma 7.9. Then Lemma 7.1 yields

$$ \lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\text{proj}})=d_{k}p_{1}\lambda_{1}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}})=\Theta(dp\tau)\cdot\left(n\mu_{1}^{2}+\tfrac{n}{d}+O(\sqrt{n}\mu_{1})\right)=o(np). $$

The last equality was obtained by (2.5). Then, plugging our estimates on $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{B}_{\proj})$ , $\lambda_{2}(\tilde{B}_{\proj})$ into (7.26) yields $\lambda_{1}(\tilde{A})-\lambda_{2}(\tilde{A})\geq\Theta(np)-o(np)$ . Applying this last inequality to (7.25) gives:

$$ \|\eta_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}\mathbf{w}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{\eta}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\left(1+\frac{\Theta(np)}{\Theta(np)-o(pn)}\right)\lesssim\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Plugging (7.28) into (7.24) and applying Proposition 4.4 to the resultant expression, we obtain

$$ d_{k}p_{1}\|\hat{Y}\hat{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}-\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim np(\tau^{2}+d\mu_{1}^{2}\Tr\Sigma)\log^{4}n+\max\{np\tau^{2},\sqrt{np}\}\log^{9}n+dp\tau\log^{4}n+\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Finally, applying Proposition 7.6 to the above display, taking dominant terms and dividing by $d_{k}p_{1}=\Theta(dp\tau)$ , produces the desired result. ∎

## 8. Proof of Frobenius and Entrywise Error Bounds

#### Proof of Corollary 2.9.

To obtain (2.10), it suffices to decompose $XX^{\mathsf{T}}$ in terms of its first $k$ eigenspaces. Recall that $X_{k}=\Pi_{X}^{(k)}X$ and $X_{k+1:d}=X-X_{k}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}+\|X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2k}\|X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+n\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{4}\Big)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2k}(\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2})+n\Big(\sum_{i>k}\mu_{i}^{4}\Big)^{1/2}. $$

Then, one can use (2.8) for the first term on the right hand side. Note that $n\mu_{k+1}^{2}=o(n\mu_{1}d^{-1/2})\leq\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)$ due to (2.7), so we can drop the $n\mu_{k+1}^{2}$ term in (8.1). This concludes the proof of (2.10). (2.11) is immediate from applying Markov’s inequality and (2.10) to obtain the mean squared error of the inner products. To prove (2.12), we first define a “signed” matrix $S=\diag(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})$ where $s_{i}=\text{sign}(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}^{2}).$ We can write the difference between norms as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}^{2}| \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}^{2})=\Tr(S(XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}})) \displaystyle=\Tr(S(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}))+\Tr(S(X_{k+1:d}X_{k+1:d}^{\mathsf{T}})) \displaystyle\leq 2k\|S(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}})\|_{\mathrm{op}}+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d} \displaystyle\leq 2k(\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+n\mu_{k+1}^{2})+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}. $$

The penultimate inequality was obtained by using the fact that $S(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}})$ is at most rank- $2k$ , the last inequality was obtained by a reverse triangle inequality, and $\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$ . Applying Markov’s inequality to the above gives (2.12), then using the inequality $(|a|-|b|)^{2}\leq|a^{2}-b^{2}|$ and again noting that $n\mu_{k+1}^{2}=o(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X))$ gives (2.13). ∎

Moreover, if one restricts the point cloud to the following good sets, we can quantify the relative recovery;

$$ \mathcal{A}(t):=\{(i,j):i\neq j,|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq t\},\qquad\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(t):=\{i\in[n]:\|x_{i}\|_{2}\geq t\}. $$

#### Corollary 8.1.

Under the same conditions as Theorem 2.5, we have that with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ , for any $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1]$ , for some sufficiently large constant $C>0$ and $t=\log^{C}n\mathcal{E}_{F}(X)n^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\delta^{-1}$

$$ \lvert\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}(t):\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle=(1+O(\delta))\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle)\}\rvert\geq\lvert\mathcal{A}(t)\rvert-\varepsilon n^{2}; $$

if $t=\log^{C/2}n\left(\frac{2k\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}{\varepsilon\delta n}\right)^{1/2}$ ,

$$ \lvert\{i\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(t):\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}=(1+O(\delta))\|x_{i}\|_{2})\}\rvert\geq|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(t)|-\varepsilon n. $$

The proof of (8.4) follows immediately from the conclusion of (2.12) and $|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle-\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle|\leq\delta\log^{C}n\cdot\mathcal{E}_{F}(X)n^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\delta^{-1}\leq\delta|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|$ , on the good pairs $(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}(\log^{C}n\cdot\mathcal{E}_{F}(X)n^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\delta^{-1})$ . $$ |\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}^{2}|\leq\log^{C}n\cdot\left(\frac{2k\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}{\varepsilon n}\right)=\delta\log^{C}n\cdot\left(\frac{2k\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{op}}(X)+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}{\varepsilon\delta n}\right)\leq\delta\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

Then we recover the difference of the norms as follows:

## 9. Proofs of Application to Random Sampling

### 9.1. Low-rank variant

We begin by stating and proving a low-rank variant of Theorem 2.16, meant as an analogue to Theorem 4.1.

#### Theorem 9.1 (Denoising with low-rank $\Sigma^{\infty}$ ).

With $n,d,p$ as in Theorem 4.1, let $X$ be the matrix whose rows are given by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ sampled independently from a distribution $\nu$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , with $\Sigma^{\infty}$ as defined in Definition 2.15 of rank $k$ . Moreover, suppose

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}, $$

$$ \esssup_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}, $$

$$ \lambda_{k}(\Sigma^{\infty})=\omega(d^{-1}). $$

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-\hat{X}\hat{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox n\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{1}d}}+\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{dnp}}\right). $$

We prove Theorem 9.1 by applying Theorem 4.1 to $\mathcal{X}$ . Let $\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^{\mathsf{T}}X$ and $\{\mu^{2}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ the singular values of $\Sigma$ , as before. We must verify that $\Sigma$ is strictly low rank and that the conditions we impose on $\Sigma^{\infty}$ imply the analogous assumptions (2.5), (2.6), (2.7) on $\Sigma$ in the statement of Theorem 4.1. $$ \big|\Sigma_{jj}-\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\big|\leq\|\Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\ \ \ \ \forall j:1\leq j\leq d, $$

$$ \bigg|\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma_{jj}-\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\bigg|\leq C\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\Tr\Sigma_{\infty,\ell:d}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\ \ \ \ \forall\ell:1\leq\ell\leq d, $$

in particular, setting $\ell=1$ in (9.6) we obtain

$$ \big|\Tr\Sigma-\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\big|\leq C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by proving (9.6). We apply Bernstein’s inequality to

$$ \sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma_{jj}-\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigg(\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}-\mathbb{E}\bigg[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\bigg]\bigg), $$

where $x_{i}\sim\nu$ are i.i.d, and $(x_{i})_{j}$ denotes the $j-$ th coordinate of $x_{i}$ . By (9.2)

$$ \Var\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\right]\leq O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\nu}\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}(x_{i})_{j}^{2}\right]=O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\left[\sum_{j=\ell}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}\right]. $$

Thus, Bernstein inequality for bounded variables and (9.2) yield (9.6).

Next, we prove (9.5) – in particular, we focus on the second inequality in (9.5) as the first is immediate from the definition of $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . Here we apply matrix Bernstein inequality (e.g.[28, Theorem 5.4.1]) to

$$ \Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}(x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty}). $$

To do so, we must verify that $\|\frac{1}{n}(x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty})\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is a bounded random variable. Note that assumption (9.2) implies that

$$ \|x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{i}-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2} $$

where we used $\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}$ . Moreover, the matrix analogue of variance satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\|\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\nu}\big(x_{i}x_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}-\Sigma^{\infty}\big)^{2}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}[\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\big]-(\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}(O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\big) \displaystyle\leq\frac{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}}{n}. $$

Therefore, we obtain

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\|\Sigma-\Sigma^{\infty}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\geq t\right)\leq 2d\exp\left(-c\min\bigg\{\frac{t^{2}n}{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})^{2}},\frac{tn}{O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})}\bigg\}\right). $$

Setting $t=C(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}$ yields the second inequality in (9.5), as desired. ∎

We are now ready check the conditions required for the application of Theorem 4.1 and complete the proof of Theorem 9.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 9.1.

First, we show that if $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is rank $k$ , then $\Sigma$ is at most rank $k$ a.s. Let $u_{1}$ , $\ldots$ , $u_{d}$ denote the eigenbasis for $\Sigma^{\infty}$ with $u_{k+1}$ , $\ldots$ , $u_{d}$ corresponding to the 0 eigenvalue. Then, for $i\geq k+1$

$$ 0=u_{i}^{T}\Sigma^{\infty}u_{i}=\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}]. $$

Since $\Sigma$ is a positive semidefinite matrix, $u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}\geq 0$ and the above identity implies $u_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma u_{i}=0$ a.s. Thus, $\dim\ker\Sigma\geq d-k$ a.s. and the desired conclusion follows.

Next we verify the following conditions (1)–(3), corresponding to (2.5)–(2.7), respectively, hold with high probability.

- (1) $\Tr\Sigma\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n}$ : This follows immediately from (9.1) and (9.7).

- (2) The point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ has no outliers ((2.6)) with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ , i.e. $\max_{i,j}\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle=O(\Tr\Sigma)$ : By (9.7) we get that there exists $C\geq 0$ such that with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$ (9.8)

$$ \Tr\Sigma\geq\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\left(1-C\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right). $$

Therefore, letting $n$ be sufficiently large (so that the right side of the above display is positive), we obtain

$$ \max_{i,j}\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\leq\esssup_{\mathbf{x}\sim\nu}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr\Sigma^{\infty})=O(\Tr\Sigma) $$

where the second inequality follows from (9.2).

- (3) $\mu_{k}^{2}=\omega(d^{-1})$ : By Weyl’s inequality and (9.5) we have $\mu_{k}^{2}\geq\lambda_{k}(\Sigma^{\infty})-C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}=\omega(d^{-1}),$ where the last relation follows by (9.3) and (9.1).

Thus, with high probability, Theorem 4.1 applies to $\mathcal{X}$ and (9.4) follows. ∎

To prove Theorem 2.16 we will check that with high probability conditions of Theorem 2.5, in place of Theorem 4.1 as in the proof of Theorem 9.1, are satisfied by the point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ .

### 9.2. Proof of Theorem 2.16

With conditions (1) and (2) as in the proof of Theorem 9.1, these properties hold with high probability by the same argument. To apply Theorem 2.5 it only remains to verify condition (2.7), that $\Sigma$ is numerically low rank, i.e. for some $k=o(\sqrt{d}/\log^{2}n)$ we have that $\mu_{k}\geq\omega(d^{-1/2})$ and $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\leq o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ .

Let $k$ be such that $\lambda_{k}(\Sigma^{\infty})\geq\omega(d^{-1})$ and $\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j}(\Sigma^{\infty})=o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ . The fact that $\mu_{k}=\omega(d^{-1/2})$ follows from the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 9.1.

The rest of this proof is dedicated to verifying that $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\leq o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ . For this argument, it is convenient to assume that $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is diagonal – we can do so without loss of generality as the properties (2.15)–(2.17) remain unchanged if we diagonalize $\Sigma^{\infty}$ . Additionally, without loss of generality we assume that $\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}\geq\ldots\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{dd}.$

By the Horn–Schur Theorem (e.g. see [19, Theorem 4.3.45 (Schur)]) and (9.6), we have that with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$

$$ \Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\leq\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma_{\ell_{j}\ell_{j}}\leq\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{\ell_{j}\ell_{j}}+C\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\Tr\Sigma_{\infty,k+1:d}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}} $$

where $\Sigma_{\ell_{1}\ell_{1}}\geq\Sigma_{\ell_{2}\ell_{2}}\geq\ldots\geq\Sigma_{\ell_{d}\ell_{d}}$ . Next, we show that with high probability $\{\ell_{k+1},\ldots,\ell_{d}\}=\{k+1,\ldots,d\}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big(\{\ell_{k+1},\ldots,\ell_{d}\}\neq \displaystyle\{k+1,\ldots,d\}\big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathbb{P}(j\in\{\ell_{k+1},\ldots,\ell_{d}\}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathbb{P}(\Sigma_{jj}<\Sigma_{\ell\ell}\text{ for some $\ell\geq k+1$}) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}\bigg[\mathbb{P}\bigg(\Sigma_{jj}<\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1,k+1}+C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\bigg) \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}\bigg(\max_{\ell\geq k+1}\Sigma_{\ell\ell}\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1,k+1}+C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\bigg)\bigg] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}\bigg[\mathbb{P}\bigg(\Sigma_{jj}<\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}-C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\bigg) \displaystyle+\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\mathbb{P}\bigg(\Sigma_{jj}\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}+C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\bigg)\bigg] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle dn^{-11}, $$

where to obtain (9.10) we observe that for all $j\leq k$

$$ \left(\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}-C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right)-\left(\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1,k+1}+C\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right)=\omega(d^{-1})>0 $$

since (2.17) implies $\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}-\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1,k+1}=\omega(d^{-1})$ and (2.15) with $d\leq n$ imply

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sqrt{dn\log n}}=o(d^{-1}). $$

Finally, (9.11) follows from (9.5).

Now we combine (9.9), (9.11) and (2.15) to get that with probability $1-O(n^{-10})$

$$ \displaystyle\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d} \displaystyle\leq\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1:d}+C\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\Tr\Sigma_{\infty,k+1:d}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}=o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right). $$

Since we showed that conditions on $\mathcal{X}$ required for application of Theorem 2.5 are satisfied, the stated result (2.18) follows if we substitute $\mu_{i}^{2}=(1+o(1))\lambda_{i}$ , $\Tr\Sigma=(1+o(1))\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}$ and $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=(1+o(1))\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}_{k+1:d}$ into (2.8). ∎

### 9.3. Proof of Corollary 2.18

By Weyl’s inequality,

$$ \lambda_{k}\geq\Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}-\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\gtrsim\Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}=\omega(d^{-1}). $$

By Horn–Schur Theorem,

$$ \sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j}\leq\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}=o\bigg(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\bigg). $$

Thus, conditions (2.15)–(2.17) are satisfied and we can apply Theorem 2.16 to $\mathcal{X}$ to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lessapprox \displaystyle n\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d\lambda_{1}}}+\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{k}}\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}\sqrt{d}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{np}}+\frac{(\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j})^{1/4}}{p}\right)\right). $$

We then substitute $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{k}$ with $\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}$ and $\Sigma^{\infty}_{kk}$ , respectively by (9.13) and because by Weyl’s inequality and the fact that $\lambda_{k}=\omega(d^{-1})$ we have

$$ \lambda_{1}\leq\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}+\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\Sigma^{\infty}_{11}. $$

Similarly, we can replace $\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\lambda_{j}$ by $\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}$ due to (9.14). ∎

### 9.4. Examples

#### 9.4.1. Sphere in $m$ dimensions

#### Lemma 9.3.

Let $x_{1}$ , $\ldots$ , $x_{n}$ denote i.i.d. samples from $\text{Unif}(R\mathcal{S}^{m-1})$ . Then, for $0\leq\varepsilon_{0}\leq\frac{1}{8}$

$$ \bigg|\bigg\{(i,j):i\neq j,|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg\}\bigg|\geq\bigg(1-\sqrt{\frac{96\log n}{(n-1)}}\bigg)\left(1-2\varepsilon_{0}-\frac{1}{m}\right)n(n-1) $$

with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$ .

#### Proof.

We begin by recalling that if $U$ is an $m\times m$ orthogonal matrix independent of $x_{i}$ then $Ux_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}x_{i}$ . Thus, if we $U$ satisfies $Ux_{j}=Re_{1}$ we get that

$$ \langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(x_{i})_{1}. $$

Let $g$ denote an $m$ -dimensional standard Gaussian vector. Using (9.15) and the fact that $x_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\frac{Rg}{\|g\|_{2}}$ , for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ we have that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg)= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|(x_{i})_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}},\|g\|_{2}\leq(1+\delta)\sqrt{m}\bigg) \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}\bigg(|g_{1}|\leq\frac{\varepsilon\|g\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}},\|g\|_{2}\geq(1+\delta)\sqrt{m}\bigg) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|g_{1}|\leq\varepsilon(1+\delta))+\exp(-\delta^{2}m/2) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\varepsilon(1+\delta)+\exp(-\delta^{2}m/2), $$

where the penultimate inequality follows by applying Gaussian concentration to $\|g\|_{2}$ . Setting $\delta=\sqrt{\frac{2\log m}{m}}$ in the above display we get that for $m\geq 2$

$$ \mathbb{P}\bigg(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\leq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\bigg)\leq 2\varepsilon+\frac{1}{m}. $$

Now, using Chernoff bound we get that for $0\leq t\leq 1$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j:j\neq i}\1\left(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\leq(1-t)\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\bigg|x_{i}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\right). $$

Next, by the Pigeonhole principle and the union bound we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sum_{i,j:j\neq i}\1\left(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\leq \displaystyle(1-t)\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\Bigg)n(n-1)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j:j\neq i}\1\left(|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|\geq\frac{\varepsilon R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\leq(1-t)\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle n\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\right)(n-1)\right), $$

and the desired result follows by setting $t=\sqrt{\frac{24\log n}{(1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m})(n-1)}}$ and noting that for $m\geq 2$ and $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{8}$ we have that $1-2\varepsilon-\frac{1}{m}\geq\frac{1}{4}.$ ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 2.20.

We begin by proving (2.24). We would like to apply Theorem 9.1 with $k=m$ . To do so, we must verify that $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is rank $m$ and assumptions (9.1)–(9.3) hold. First, note that

$$ \Sigma^{\infty}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\text{Unif}R\mathcal{S}^{m-1}}\bigg[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigg]=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{R^{2}}{m}I_{m}&O_{d-m}\\
O_{d-m}&O_{d-m}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $I_{m}$ is the $m\times m$ identity matrix and $O_{d-m}$ is the $(d-m)\times(d-m)$ matrix of all 0s. Thus, $\Sigma^{\infty}$ is rank $m$ and $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=R^{2}.$ Hence, (9.1) is satisfied by assumption that $R^{2}\lesssim 1/(\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n)$ . Additionally, $\max_{i,j}\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\leq R^{2}=\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}$ . Thus, (9.2) holds. Finally, $\lambda_{m}(\Sigma^{\infty})=\frac{R^{2}}{m}$ , thus $\lambda_{m}(\Sigma^{\infty})=\omega(d^{-1})$ by assumption $R^{2}=\omega(\frac{m}{d})$ and, therefore, (9.3) is satisfied as well. Consequently, we may apply Theorem 9.1 to $\mathcal{X}$ .

Now we estimate the spectral quantities that appear in the bound we get from a direct application of Theorem 9.1 to $\mathcal{X}$ . To this end, we relate $\lambda_{1}(XX^{\mathsf{T}})$ , $\lambda_{m}(XX^{\mathsf{T}})$ and $\|X\|_{F}^{2}$ to the corresponding spectral statistics of $n\Sigma^{\infty}$ using Lemma 9.2. By Weyl’s inequality with (9.5) and (9.7)

$$ \lambda_{i}(XX^{\mathsf{T}})=\lambda_{i}(X^{\mathsf{T}}X)=\frac{nR^{2}}{m}+O\bigg(R^{2}\sqrt{n\log n}\bigg)=(1+o(1))\frac{nR^{2}}{m},\text{ for all }1\leq i\leq m, $$

since our assumptions imply $\omega(m)=\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log n}<\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$ . Specifically, this tells us that $\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=(1+o(1))nR^{2}/m$ and $\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{F}=(1+o(1))nR^{2}/\sqrt{m}$ . Now, setting $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{k}=R^{2}/m$ , $k=m$ and $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=R^{2}$ in Theorem 9.1 and using the fact that $\omega(m/d)=R^{2}$ we obtain (2.24). The Frobenius bound is immediately obtained using the fact that $XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is at most rank $-2m$ . We now prove (2.26). By (2.24), and (9.17) we have that for some $C>0$

$$ \|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\log^{C}n\cdot\frac{nR^{2}}{m}\left(\frac{\sqrt{m}}{R\sqrt{d}}+\sqrt{d}R^{2}+\frac{m}{R^{2}\sqrt{npd}}\right):=(\mathcal{E}_{\infty})_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Note that the constant $C$ in (2.11) and (2.12) are meant to account for the constant from the above display, so they are the same. Let

$$ \varepsilon_{n}=\log^{C/2}n\cdot(\mathcal{E}_{\infty})^{1/2}_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{\sqrt{2m}}{\sqrt{n}R}. $$

Then set $\varepsilon_{n}=\varepsilon$ from (2.12). Combining the above display with our assumptions (2.25), we get that $\varepsilon_{n}=o(1)$ . Therefore all but $n\varepsilon_{n}$ indices satisfy $|\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}^{2}-R^{2}|<\varepsilon_{n}R^{2}$ , and consequently $\|x_{i}^{G}\|_{2}=(1+O(\varepsilon_{n}))R$ for all but $o(n)$ indices. We now prove (2.27). First, we use $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{n}^{2}$ as an input to (2.11), the lower bound on the inner product difference in the set (2.11) is then

$$ \frac{\log^{C}n}{n\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}^{2}}}\cdot\sqrt{2m}(\mathcal{E}_{\infty})_{\mathrm{op}}=\frac{\sqrt{m}R^{2}\varepsilon_{n}^{2}}{m\varepsilon_{n}}=\varepsilon_{n}\frac{R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}. $$

Consequently, taking the complement of (2.11) with the above lower bound, we obtain that

$$ |\mathcal{G}|:=\bigg\lvert\left\{(i,j):i\neq j,|\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle-\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|<\varepsilon_{n}\frac{R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right\}\Bigg\rvert\geq n(n-1)-\varepsilon_{n}^{2}n^{2}. $$

Now, let $\mathcal{A}(\frac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}})$ be defined as in Equation 8.3, where $\varepsilon_{0}\in(0,\frac{1}{8}]$ . By Lemma 9.3, we know that with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$ ,

$$ \left|\mathcal{A}\left(\tfrac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\right|\geq\bigg(1-\sqrt{\frac{96\log n}{n-1}}\bigg)\bigg(1-2\varepsilon_{0}-\frac{1}{m}\bigg)n(n-1). $$

Thus, for a pair on indices in the intersection of $\mathcal{A}(\frac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}})$ and $\mathcal{G}$ ,

$$ |\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle-\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|<\varepsilon_{n}\frac{R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{n}}{\varepsilon_{0}}|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|, $$

so $\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle=(1+o_{\varepsilon_{0}}(1))\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle$ , since $\varepsilon_{0}$ is fixed and $\varepsilon_{n}=o(1)$ . Finally, combining (9.20) and (9.21), we count the indices in the intersection:

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{A}(\tfrac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}})\cap\mathcal{G}| \displaystyle\geq|\mathcal{A}(\tfrac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}})|-\big(n(n-1)-|\mathcal{G}|\big) \displaystyle\geq|\mathcal{A}(\tfrac{\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}{\sqrt{m}})|-\varepsilon_{n}^{2}n^{2}\geq\bigg(1-2\varepsilon_{0}-\frac{1}{m}-o(1)\bigg)n(n-1), $$

which gives us (2.27). ∎

#### 9.4.3. Sinusoid curve

#### Proof of Proposition 2.25.

Here we will use Corollary 2.18, as $\Sigma^{\infty}$ turns out to be a numerically low rank approximately diagonal matrix. We begin by proving (2.34) by computing $\Sigma^{\infty}$ . Using the product-to-sum trigonometric identity $\cos(a)\cos(b)=\frac{1}{2}(\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b))$ , we obtain for $i\neq j$ (also noting that our assumption (2.32) implies that $\omega_{i}\neq\omega_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ )

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\infty}_{ij} \displaystyle=a_{i}a_{j}\int_{[0,1]}\cos(\omega_{i}t+\phi_{i})\cos(\omega_{j}t+\phi_{j})dt \displaystyle=\frac{a_{i}a_{j}}{2}\int_{[0,1]}\cos((\omega_{i}-\omega_{j})t+\phi_{i}-\phi_{j})dt+\frac{a_{i}a_{j}}{2}\int_{[0,1]}\cos((\omega_{i}+\omega_{j})t+\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})dt \displaystyle=\frac{a_{i}a_{j}}{2}\left(\frac{\sin((\omega_{i}-\omega_{j})+\phi_{i}-\phi_{j})-\sin(\phi_{i}-\phi_{j})}{\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}}+\frac{\sin((\omega_{i}+\omega_{j})+\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})-\sin(\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})}{\omega_{i}+\omega_{j}}\right). $$

Similarly, the diagonal entries:

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\infty}_{ii} \displaystyle=a_{i}^{2}\int_{[0,1]}\cos^{2}(\omega_{i}t+\phi_{i})dt \displaystyle=a_{i}^{2}\frac{1}{2}+a_{i}^{2}\frac{\sin(2(\omega_{i}+\phi_{i}))-\sin(2\phi_{i})}{4\omega_{i}}. $$

Notice that we can write

$$ \Sigma^{\infty}=\frac{1}{2}\diag\Bigg(a_{1}^{2}\left(1+\frac{\sin(2(\omega_{1}+\phi_{1}))-\sin(2\phi_{1})}{2\omega_{1}}\right),\dots,a_{d}^{2}\left(1+\frac{\sin(2(\omega_{d}+\phi_{d}))-\sin(2\phi_{d})}{2\omega_{d}}\right)\Bigg)+E, $$

where $E$ is defined to have entries

$$ \displaystyle E_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{a_{i}a_{j}}{2}\left(\frac{\sin((\omega_{i}-\omega_{j})+\phi_{i}-\phi_{j})-\sin(\phi_{i}-\phi_{j})}{\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}}+\frac{\sin((\omega_{i}+\omega_{j})+\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})-\sin(\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})}{\omega_{i}+\omega_{j}}\right) $$

for $i\neq j$ and $E_{ii}=0$ for $1\leq i\leq d$ . Applying triangle inequality to the above display we get that,

$$ |E_{ij}|\leq\begin{cases}a_{i}a_{j}\left(\frac{1}{|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|}+\frac{1}{|\omega_{i}+\omega_{j}|}\right)\quad\text{ if }i\neq j,\\
0\qquad\text{ if }i=j\end{cases}. $$

Recall $\Omega=\min_{i\neq j}||\omega_{i}|-|\omega_{j}||$ , and that by assumption $a_{1}=\max_{i}|a_{i}|$ . By the Schur test (see (7.16)),

$$ \|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\max_{i}\sum_{j}|E_{ij}|\lesssim\frac{a_{1}^{2}d}{\Omega}. $$

Notice, that our assumption (2.33) gives us $\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\tfrac{1}{d}$ , satisfying the “approximately diagonal” condition in the statement of Corollary 2.18.

We check the other conditions of Corollary 2.18. For condition (2.20) to be satisfied, we note that is deduced from the minimum assumption on the frequencies (2.33) :

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{1}{2}\Bigg(a_{i}^{2}\bigg(1+\frac{\sin(2(\omega_{i}+\phi_{i}))-\sin(2\phi_{i})}{2\omega_{i}}\bigg)\Bigg)\lesssim\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\omega_{i}|}\right)\lesssim\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}. $$

The last step is obtained by (2.33), since that assumption implies that $1+1/|\omega_{i}|\lesssim 1$ . Note that the same steps can be repeated, by using the lower bound on $\sin(y)\geq-1$ , to obtain $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\gtrsim\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{|\omega_{i}|}\right)\gtrsim\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}$ . (9.27) and the lower bound computation imply

$$ \Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=\Theta\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\right). $$

Combining (9.27) with (2.30), gives us the upper bound assumptions on $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}$ –(2.20).

Condition (2.21) is now trivially satisfied, by $-1\leq\cos(y)\leq 1$ and (9.28):

$$ \|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega_{i}T+\phi_{i})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}. $$

Condition (2.22) follows from our assumptions $k=o(\sqrt{d}/\log^{2}n)$ and (2.32). Then, the assumption on the tail (2.22), can be inferred by the fact that $\Tr E=0$ and (2.31) Therefore, Corollary 2.18 applies and the inequality (2.34) follows. We defer the proof of (2.38) below, as we will need Lemma 9.6. ∎

#### Remark 9.4.

One could also sample frequencies in the window of length $n^{10}d\Omega:=\Omega^{\prime}$

$$ \omega_{i}\sim\text{Unif}\big[1,\Omega^{\prime}\big], $$

where recall $\Omega$ is the minimum frequency gap, of the same order as specified in (2.33). Using an elementary order statistics computation (see Lemma 9.5 for more details), we can find the probability of the smallest gap explicitly. For $t(d-1)\leq d\cdot\Omega$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\min_{i<j}|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|\geq t\right)=\left(1-\frac{(d-1)t}{\Omega^{\prime}}\right)^{d}. $$

In our example, we require the gap to be of order greater than $\Omega\gtrsim a^{2}d^{2}$ , setting $t=\Omega$ gives us that with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$ ,

$$ \min_{i<j}|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|\geq\Omega=\omega\left(a^{2}d^{2}\right). $$

#### Lemma 9.5.

If $\omega_{1},\dots\omega_{d}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}\text{Unif}{[a,b]}$ then

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\min_{i\neq j}|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|\geq t\right)=\begin{cases}\left(\frac{b-a-t(d-1)}{b-a}\right)^{d}\quad\text{ for }t(d-1)\leq b-a,\\
0\quad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

Let $\omega_{(i)}$ be the $(i)$ -th order statistic. Since $\omega_{i}$ ’s are identically distributed, we know that the joint probability density of $\omega_{(1)},\dots\omega_{(d)}$ is $d!\frac{1}{(b-a)^{d}}$ . To compute our desired probability, it suffices to evaluate the following integral:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\min_{i\neq j}|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|\geq t\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\omega_{(1)}<\omega_{(2)}-t,\dots,\omega_{(d-1)}<\omega_{(d)}-t\right) \displaystyle=\frac{d!}{(b-a)^{d}}\int_{a+(d-1)t}^{b-t}\dots\int_{a+t}^{x_{3}-t}\int_{a}^{x_{2}-t}1dx_{1}dx_{2}\dots dx_{d} $$

Making the change of variables $y_{i}=x_{i}-(i-1)t$ gives the result. ∎

#### Lemma 9.6.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be as in Proposition 2.25, satisfying (2.30)–(2.33), and assume additionally that (2.36). Then, on the same event on which (2.34) and (2.35) hold, we have that for some constants $c,c_{1}>0$ , with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$

$$ \Big|\Big\{i\in[n]:\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq c\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\Big\}\Big|\geq\bigg(1-\sqrt{\frac{44\log n}{n}}\bigg)\bigg(1-\frac{c_{1}}{k}\bigg)n. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 9.6.

The proof will rely on an application of a Chernoff bound on the indicators of large enough $\|x_{i}\|_{2}$ ’s. To this end, we first estimate the probability of $\mathbb{P}(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\leq O(\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}))$ , by Tchebyshev’s inequality, thus we estimate the variance of $\|x_{i}\|_{2}=\|(a_{j}\cos(\omega_{j}T_{i}+\phi_{j}))_{j=1}^{d}\|_{2}$ , for $T_{i}\sim\text{Unif}{[0,1]}$ . (2.36) and the simplification $a_{1}\geq\dots\geq a_{d}\geq 0$ imply that

$$ \sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\geq\sum_{j\leq k}a_{j}^{2}\geq ka_{k}^{2}\gtrsim ka_{1}^{2},\qquad\text{thus }k=\omega(1)\text{ gives }\qquad a_{1}^{2}=o\Big(\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\Big). $$

By the double angle identity $\cos^{2}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}(1+\cos(2\theta))$ , we can find an explicit expression for the norm

$$ \|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\cos(2\omega_{j}T_{i}+2\phi_{j}), $$

and therefore for any $1\leq i\leq n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Var\big(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\big) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}_{T_{i}\sim\text{Unif}{[0,1]}}\bigg[\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\cos(2\omega_{j}T_{i}+2\phi_{j})\Big)^{2}\bigg] \displaystyle=\;\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j,l=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}a_{l}^{2}\int_{[0,1]}\cos(2\omega_{j}t+2\phi_{j})\cos(2\omega_{l}t+2\phi_{l})dt. $$

Following the same computation as in (9.24) yields for $j\neq l$

$$ \bigg|\int_{[0,1]}\cos(2\omega_{j}t+2\phi_{j})\cos(2\omega_{l}t+2\phi_{l})\,dt\bigg|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{2|\omega_{j}-\omega_{l}|}+\frac{1}{2|\omega_{j}+\omega_{l}|}\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\Omega}. $$

For $j=l$ , the integral is $\leq 1$ . Then using (2.33) and $\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\leq da_{1}^{2}$ ,

$$ \Var\left(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\right)\lesssim\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{4}+\frac{1}{\Omega}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\right)^{2}\leq a_{1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}+\frac{1}{a_{1}^{2}d^{2}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\right)^{2}\leq a_{1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}+\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\lesssim a_{1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}. $$

The last inequality was obtained by using (2.32) to conclude that $a_{1}^{2}\geq a_{k}^{2}=\omega(1/d)$ . Then, applying (9.30) to the above, yields for all $1\leq i\leq n$

$$ \Var\big(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\big)\lesssim\frac{1}{k}\Big(\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\Big)^{2}. $$

Due to (9.31), we know that $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=\Theta\big(\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}^{2}\big)$ . This implies that there exists a constant $c_{0}>0$ (not dependent on the index $i$ ) such that $\mathbb{E}\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}\geq c_{0}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}$ ). Then Tchebyshev’s inequality combined with (9.33) gives, for some $c_{1}>0$

$$ q:=\mathbb{P}\left(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{c_{0}}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\right)\geq 1-\frac{\Var\left(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{c_{0}}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\right)^{2}}\geq 1-\frac{c_{1}}{k}=1-o(1), $$

where the last inequality was obtained by (2.36). By independence of $T_{1},\dots,T_{n}$ , we know that $\1\big(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}<\frac{c_{0}}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\big)\sim\text{Bern}(q)$ . Thus, by a Chernoff bound, we have that

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\1\left(\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{c_{0}}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\right)\leq(1-t)nq\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}nq\right). $$

(9.34) gives that for large enough $n$ , $q\geq 1/2$ , so setting $t=\sqrt{22\log n/(nq)}$ , implies that the right-hand side of (9.35) is $\leq n^{-11}$ , so with probability at least $1-n^{-11}$ ,

$$ \bigg|\bigg\{i\in[n]:\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{c_{0}}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{d}a_{l}^{2}\bigg\}\bigg|\geq(1-t)nq\geq\bigg(1-\sqrt{\frac{44\log n}{n}}\bigg)\bigg(1-\frac{c_{1}}{k}\bigg)n, $$

where in the last step we used (9.34), (2.36) and $\log n=o(n)$ . Taking $c=c_{0}/2$ concludes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of (2.38).

Throughout this proof, we will condition on the intersection of the events on which Equation 2.35 and Lemma 9.6 hold, which by a union bound, occurs with probability at least $1-O(n^{-10})$ . In particular, by Lemma 9.6, all but $o(n)$ of the points satisfy $\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq c\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}$ , so by Corollary 8.1 with $\varepsilon=\delta$ (for simplicity) and $t=\big(c\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\big)^{1/2}$ , it suffices to show that

$$ \frac{2k\|XX^{\mathsf{T}}-X_{G}X_{G}^{\mathsf{T}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+n\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}na_{j}^{2}}=o(1). $$

(2.38) then holds for all but $o(n)$ of the indices with $\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\geq c\sum_{j}a_{j}^{2}$ , hence for all but $o(n)$ indices in $[n]$ . For the first summand being $o(1)$ is an immediate consequence of (2.37), (2.36) and (9.30). As for the second summand, (9.6) implies that with probability at least $1-O(n^{-11})$

$$ \Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}\leq\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}^{\infty}\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}+\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}^{\infty} $$

The Horn–Schur theorem applied to (9.26), together with $\Sigma^{\infty}_{jj}=\tfrac{1}{2}a_{j}^{2}\big(1+O(|\omega_{j}|^{-1})\big)\lesssim a_{j}^{2}$ and $\Tr\Sigma^{\infty}=\Theta\big(\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}\big)$ from (9.27), implies that $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}^{\infty}\lesssim\sum_{j>k}a_{j}^{2}$ . Plugging the former into (9.37), and dividing by $\sum_{j}^{d}a_{j}^{2}$ gives

$$ \frac{\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}}\lesssim\frac{\sum_{j>k}a_{j}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}}+\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{j>k}a_{j}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_{j}^{2}}\frac{\log n}{n}}=o(1/k)+o(1). $$

The last equality was obtained by (2.32), and (2.31). ∎

Under the same assumptions as Proposition 2.25, on the same event for which (2.35) holds, and for every $t=\omega\big(n^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{F}(X))_{\infty}\big)$ ,

$$ \bigl|\bigl\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}(t):\langle x_{i}^{G},x_{j}^{G}\rangle=(1+o(1))\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\bigr\}\bigr|\geq|\mathcal{A}(t)|-o(n^{2}), $$

where $(\mathcal{E}_{F})_{\infty}$ denotes the right hand side of (2.35) (by substituting (2.34) into (2.35)), and $\mathcal{A}$ is defined as in (8.3).

#### Proof of Proposition 9.7.

## Appendix A Parameter Estimation Proofs and Asymptotics

With the exception of the proof of Lemma 4.2 in Section A.5, the parameter estimates below are stated and proved for the truncated (strictly rank- $k$ ) model, i.e. in terms of the truncated adjacency matrix $\tilde{A}$ and the associated edge density $\tilde{p}$ . This entails no loss of generality for the numerically low-rank setting of Theorem 2.5. In the strictly rank- $k$ case $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=0$ , so $\tilde{A}=A$ and $\tilde{p}=p$ . In the numerically low-rank case the tail hypothesis $\Tr\Sigma_{k+1:d}=o\left(\min(p^{3},d^{-1})\right)$ guarantees, via Lemma 7.9, that $p=(1+o(1))\tilde{p}$ , so every estimate proved here for $\tilde{p}$ holds for $p$ up to a $(1+o(1))$ factor and the leading-order asymptotics are unchanged.

### A.1. Proof of Lemma 6.2

Recall the decomposition of the noisy vectors $\tilde{y}_{i}=(a_{i},w_{i})$ where $a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ represents the signal plus noise, and $w_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}$ is the noise. We further decompose the signal vector as $a_{i}=\Pi^{(k)}_{X}x_{i}+N_{i}=\tilde{x}_{i}+N_{i}$ , where $x_{i}$ is the fixed point cloud vector and $N_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{k})$ . The inner product expands as:

$$ \left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle=\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle N_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle+\left\langle N_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle. $$

Using Bernstein’s inequality (e.g. see [28, Theorem 2.8.1]), and the fact that for each entry of the vector $N_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , we have that $\|(N_{i})_{l}\|_{\psi_{2}}=O(1/\sqrt{d})$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left({\exists(i,j)\in[n]^{2},i\neq j:\langle N_{i},N_{j}\rangle\geq t}\right)\leq e^{2\log n-c_{1}\min(td,t^{2}d^{2}/k)}. $$

We require $2\log n<c_{1}\min(td,t^{2}d^{2}/k)$ , so if $k<\log n$ , set $t=C_{1}\frac{\log n}{d}$ , or if $k>\log n$ then $t=C_{1}\frac{\sqrt{k\log n}}{d}$ for some $C_{1}>0$ . Thus, it follows that $\left\langle N_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle\leq C_{1}\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}$ with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ , for $C_{1}$ sufficiently large uniformly over all pairs $(i,j)\in[n]^{2},i\neq j$ .

By (2.6) and Cauchy-Schwartz,

$$ |\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{x}_{j}\right\rangle|\leq\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|_{2}\|\tilde{x}_{j}\|_{2}\leq\|x_{i}\|_{2}\|x_{j}\|_{2}\leq\Tr\Sigma. $$

When $i\neq j$ , the cross-term $\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle$ is a mean zero, Gaussian variable with variance $\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|^{2}/d\lesssim\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)/d$ . Therefore, with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ , $|\left\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{j}\right\rangle|\lesssim\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\log n/d}$ and thus

$$ \left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle=O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right). $$

While it is tempting to bound the right hand side by the simpler expression $O(\Tr\Sigma\cdot\log n)$ (using (2.7)), in some of the arguments below we cannot afford to lose a logarithmic factor.

On the other hand, for the $i=j$ case, the expression (A.1) becomes

$$ \|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\tilde{x}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle\tilde{x}_{i},N_{i}\rangle+\|N_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

By [28, Theorem 3.1.1], we know that with probability at least $1-n^{-12}$ ,

$$ \|N_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O\left(\frac{k}{d}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right). $$

Applying the condition (2.6) as in the case $i\neq j$ , we obtain

$$ \|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O\left(\Tr\Sigma+\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{k}{d}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}}}{d}\right)\leq O(\Tr\Sigma\log n). $$

For the lengths $l_{i}=\|w_{i}\|_{2}$ , note that $d\|w_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{d_{k}}$ . $\|\chi_{d_{k}}^{2}-d_{k}\|_{\psi_{1}}=\sqrt{d_{k}}$ , therefore by Bernstein’s inequality,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\exists i\in[n]:|l_{i}^{2}-d_{k}/d|>t\right)\leq e^{\log n-c\min\{\frac{t^{2}d^{2}}{d_{k}},\frac{td}{d_{k}}\}}. $$

Setting $t=C_{3}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}$ for $C_{3}>0$ large enough gives

$$ l_{i}=1+O\left(\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\right). $$

Thus, the product becomes

$$ l_{i}l_{j}=1+O(\sqrt{\log n}/\sqrt{d}). $$

∎

### A.2. Proof of Lemma 6.3

Let $\psi_{X}(t):=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\mathbb{P}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq t/\sqrt{d})$ , and let $\tau(p)=\tau_{X}(p)$ be the unique value of $\tau$ such that $p=\psi_{X}(\tau\sqrt{d})$ .

#### Lemma A.1.

Let $\Psi(t):=\mathbb{P}(g\geq t)$ denote the complementary distribution function for a standard Gaussian variable on $\mathbb{R}$ . Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.5,

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{d}\tau_{X}(p) \displaystyle=\Psi^{-1}(p)+O\bigg(\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma+(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n+\frac{\log^{2}n}{\sqrt{d}}\bigg) \displaystyle=\Psi^{-1}(p)+\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma)\,. $$

Note that $\Psi^{-1}(p)=\sqrt{2\log(1/p)}(1+O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}))$ .

#### Proof.

Set $\mathcal{E}:=\sqrt{d}\Tr\Sigma+(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n+\frac{\log^{2}n}{\sqrt{d}}$ . It will suffice to show that for all $i\neq j$ and $T\in[\frac{1}{100},\log n]$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle\geq T/\sqrt{d})=\Psi(T+O(\mathcal{E}))+O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})\,. $$

Indeed, we have that $\psi_{X}$ is strictly decreasing, and from (A.7),

$$ \psi_{X}(T)=\Psi(T+O(\mathcal{E})) $$

for $T\in[\frac{1}{100},\log n]$ . From this and the monotonicity of $\psi_{X}$ and $\Psi$ (noting that $\Psi(\log n)<p<\Psi(\frac{1}{100})$ ) we verify $\sqrt{d}\tau_{X}(p)=\Psi^{-1}(p)+O(\mathcal{E})$ , as desired.

It remains to establish (A.7). By relabeling indices we may assume $(i,j)=(1,2)$ . Letting $g:=\langle z_{1}/\|z_{1}\|_{2},z_{2}\rangle$ , we have

$$ \langle y_{1},y_{2}\rangle=\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle+\langle x_{1},z_{2}\rangle+\langle x_{2},z_{1}\rangle+\|z_{1}\|_{2}g. $$

From Cauchy–Schwarz and (2.6) it follows

$$ |\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle|\leq\|x_{1}\|_{2}\|x_{2}\|_{2}\lesssim\Tr\Sigma\,. $$

Next note that $\langle x_{1},z_{2}\rangle\sim N(0,\|x_{1}\|_{2}^{2}/d)$ , so again from (2.6) it follows

$$ \langle x_{1},z_{2}\rangle\lesssim d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ . The same holds for $\langle x_{2},z_{1}\rangle$ . Finally, since $d\|z_{1}\|_{2}^{2}$ is a sum of independent uniformly sub-exponential variables of expectation 1, we find

$$ \|z_{1}\|_{2}=1+O(\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}}) $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ . Combining these estimates, we have that

$$ \langle y_{1},y_{2}\rangle=(1+O(\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}}))g+O(\Tr\Sigma+d^{-1/2}(\Tr\Sigma)^{1/2}\log n) $$

with probability $1-O(e^{-c\log^{2}n})$ , from which (A.7) follows. ∎

### A.3. Proof of Lemma 6.4

Before commencing with the proof we recall some facts related to the Gegenbauer polynomial basis.

We will use the random variable $\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d}$ , to denote the distribution of $\sqrt{d}\langle u,w\rangle$ where $u$ and $w$ are independent vectors distributed uniformly on the unit sphere $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ . The scaling factor $\sqrt{d}$ ensures that the second moment is normalized $\mathbb{E}[\xi^{2}]=1$ . The probability density function of $\xi$ is given by

$$ f_{d}(\xi)=\frac{\Gamma(d/2)}{\sqrt{d\pi}\Gamma((d-1)/2)}\left(1-\frac{\xi^{2}}{d}\right)^{\frac{d-3}{2}}. $$

This density function serves as the weight function for the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{q_{k}^{(d)}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ , which form an orthonormal basis for the space $L^{2}([-\sqrt{d},\sqrt{d}],\mathcal{D}_{d})$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d}}[q_{k}^{(d)}(\xi)q_{l}^{(d)}(\xi)]=\delta_{kl}. $$

Note that they can be obtained by applying the Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization process to the monomial basis. The Gegenbauer polynomials can be expressed as a linear combination of spherical harmonics, which results in the following identity: for $u,w,v$ independent and uniform in $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{v}[q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle u,v\rangle)q_{j}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle v,w\rangle)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{l}^{(d)}}}1_{l=j}q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d}\langle u,w\rangle). $$

Moreover, from orthonormality, we can obtain that

$$ q_{l}^{(d)}(\sqrt{d})=\sqrt{N_{l}^{(d)}}. $$

#### Proof.

We first estimate the size of $\tau^{ij}$ using Lemma 6.3. Recall that the shifted threshold is defined as $\tau^{ij}=(\tau-\left\langle a_{i},a_{j}\right\rangle)/(l_{i}l_{j})$ . Here however, to be more accurate, we use the full estimates on $\langle a_{i},a_{j}\rangle$ without adding extra logarithmic factors, as in the proof of Lemma 6.4. Plugging in the first expression (A.2), and (A.6). Plugging these estimates into the expression for $\tau^{ij}$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\tau^{ij} \displaystyle=\left(\tau-O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right)\right)\left(1+O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right)\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=\left(\tau-O\left(\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)+\sqrt{\Tr\left(\Sigma\right)\frac{\log n}{d}}+\frac{\sqrt{\max\{k,\log n\}\log n}}{d}\right)\right)\left(1-O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}}\right)\right). $$

The last line was obtained by a Taylor expansion. Then, using (2.5) and Lemma 6.3, the dominant term is $\tau^{ij}=\tau+O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\log n})$ . Note that the same computation works for $i=j$ since both $\langle a_{i},a_{j}\rangle=O(\Tr\Sigma\log n)$ and $\|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\Tr\Sigma\log n)$ from Lemma 6.2.

Recall that $p_{0}^{ij}$ and $p_{1}^{ij}$ correspond to the 0-th and 1-st Gegenbauer coefficients of the expansion of the kernel function $\1(\sqrt{d_{k}}\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{ij})$ , since $\tau^{ij}$ is of the same order of magnitude as in [21], the proof for $p_{0},p_{1}p_{0}^{ij}$ and $p_{1}^{ij}$ follows verbatim as in their Lemma 4.9 [21], which is a direct computation. However, for the benefit of subsequent proofs, we outline explicit expressions for $p_{1}$ below:

$$ \displaystyle p_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d_{k}}}[\xi\mathbf{1}(\xi\geq\sqrt{d_{k}}\tau)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\int_{\sqrt{d_{k}}\tau}^{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\xi f(\xi)d\xi, $$

where $f=f_{d_{k}}$ is the density function of $\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d_{k}}$ (see (A.8)). Note that we can evaluate the integral for $p_{1}$ explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle p_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{D}_{d_{k}}}[\xi\1(\xi\geq\sqrt{d_{k}}\tau)]=\frac{\Gamma(d_{k}/2)}{d_{k}\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma((d_{k}-1)/2)}\int_{\sqrt{d_{k}}\tau}^{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\left(1-\frac{\xi^{2}}{d_{k}}\right)^{\frac{d_{k}-3}{2}}\xi d\xi \displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(d_{k}/2)}{d_{k}\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma((d_{k}-1)/2)}\frac{d_{k}}{d_{k}-1}(1-\xi^{2}/d_{k})^{\frac{d_{k}-1}{2}}\Bigg|_{\sqrt{d_{k}}\tau}^{\sqrt{d_{k}}}=\frac{\Gamma(d_{k}/2)}{(d_{k}-1)\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma((d_{k}-1)/2)}(1-\tau^{2})^{\frac{d_{k}-1}{2}}. $$
